thesis: Order by downstream fanout, not by difficulty or category — but gate every rule on an induction base and gate every card on a validated ear, because an SRS review strengthens the phonological trace you had at encoding rather than repairing it. The five analyses converge on one braid: ~2 weeks of pure discrimination before card 1, a vocabulary track capped at 20 new/day (the review-load arithmetic everyone uses is wrong by ~3x and 6,000 words by month 9 is not reachable at 1-2 h/day), a closed-set grammar sprint that opens at ~500 recognized words and retires on a 140-item audio battery by month 9, and an input regime that ignites on a timed comprehension test at ~350 morae/min rather than on a word count. Where the dependency graph and the interference analysis fight — potential and transitivity pairs both want the -eru slot, relative clauses and nominalization both want to be first — the tiebreak is always the same: the ear has one cue, so the item whose disambiguator survives in the audio stream goes first and its homophone waits five weeks.

laws.name: Perception gates encoding
laws.statement: No lexical item is admitted until the contrasts that distinguish words are categorical percepts. Vowel length, gemination, and moraic N gate absolutely. Pitch accent does not gate, but it is a card-format constraint from card 1.
laws.mechanism: An SRS review strengthens the phonological trace you held at encoding; it does not repair it. If kite / kiite / kitte collapse into one blurred form, every review deepens the blur, and the learner does not store a fuzzy word — they store the same form three times with contradictory meanings. Length is phonemic and functionally loaded (ojiisan/ojisan, shitte/shite, biru/biiru, kookoo/koko), so the collapse destroys lexical identity, not naturalness. Accent is different in kind: it is a per-word lexical property, acquired far more cheaply distributed across 6,000 items than concentrated in 60 pairs — but it must be present at first encoding or you pay a second full pass over the lexicon plus a re-recording of the deck.
laws.consequence: 10-14 days of pure high-variability discrimination before card 1, hard ceiling 4 weeks, tiered exit (>=85% on novel talkers releases; 75-85% releases with a 10 min/day continuing track; below 75% at 4 weeks releases anyway with monthly re-test) — because HVPT on Japanese length plateaus around 80-85% on unheard voices and a 90% gate can trap a learner for two months. Every noun's audio is recorded as 'X ga' from item 1, because heiban [0] and odaka are acoustically identical on the bare word and differ only in whether the particle drops. And the TTS pipeline is validated against an accent reference before a single card is generated — off-the-shelf Japanese TTS is unreliable on lexical accent, which makes the whole accent-tagging plan unfalsifiable if skipped.

laws.name: Fanout-weighted topological sort, with a bootstrapping override
laws.statement: Among nodes whose prerequisites are satisfied, take the one that maximizes (size of downstream subtree x conversational-token frequency) — never the easiest, never the one that completes a tidy category. Override: items that let you extract further items from a native speaker in real time jump the queue regardless of their own frequency.
laws.mechanism: Grammar for a listener is a gating problem, not an accumulation problem. Unlocking a node with fanout N does not add one construction to your output; it converts N constructions in the incoming stream from unparseable noise into partially parseable structure. The -te form has roughly 35 direct dependents (approximate — the commonly cited 45 double-counts second-order nodes hanging off -te iru and items taught inside the -te unit itself), which is still about double the runner-up. Separately, 'X tte nani?' and 'nihongo de nan te iimasu ka' change the shape of the acquisition curve rather than a point on it: without them vocabulary arrives only from prepared material, with them every conversation becomes an item source.
laws.consequence: The -te chant gets the largest single time budget in the course and lands the week its induction base closes. Adjective inflection (fanout ~8, no subtree) loses every scheduling contest against the -te subtree — except its -ku/-kunai core, which is pulled forward because -ku naru, -te hoshikunai, -kereba, -sugiru, -soo, and -yasui all need it and the standard plan violates its own DAG by using them before teaching it. And 'X tte nani?' is item ~30, roughly 400 items before the quotative -tte it contains.

laws.name: The citation form is the form in the signal
laws.statement: Whatever sits on the prompt side of the card gets automatized, and the audio stream contains the reduced form. Therefore the contraction is the citation form and the long form is the labelled formal expansion.
laws.mechanism: A reading-first learner can afford the long form because the page always shows it. A listener cannot: training on -te iru inserts a real-time decompression step into every act of listening, and decompression is exactly the operation that fails first under working-memory load. Critically, reductions come in two perceptually distinct kinds. Mora-DELETING: te iru > teru (-1), te oku > toku (-1), te shimau > chau (-2), te iku > teku (-1). Mora-PRESERVING segmental substitution: wakaranai > wakannai (5 morae to 5 morae, ra assimilating to the following nasal), suru no > sun no, -ui > -ii (samui > samii, atsui > atsii). Only the first is a shortening. The second keeps the rhythm identical and swaps a segment, which is harder to hear and needs a different drill entirely.
laws.consequence: -teru, -temasu, -nakya, -nakucha, -cha, -ja, -chau, -toku, -tte, -n da are the primary forms at introduction; -te iru, -nakereba naranai, -te wa ikenai, de wa nai, to iu are taught alongside as formal expansions. Then a dedicated systematizing pass at month 10 presents them as a handful of phonological processes split by the two kinds, so the learner can correctly guess a reduction they have never heard.

laws.name: One grammar, two shells, split by channel
laws.statement: Teach the plain grammar once. Comprehend plain from the first verb; produce -masu/-desu for the first four months. Politeness is a suffix shell, not a second curriculum.
laws.mechanism: Politeness surfaces almost entirely on the final predicate, so clause-internal structure is register-invariant — but the plain-form lock is narrower than the usual claim. Plain is obligatory in prenominal (relative and noun-complement), quotative, nominalized, and conditional/temporal positions: roughly 25 constructions. It is fully optional before kara, node, kedo, ga, and shi ('Ame ga furimasu kara, yamemashoo' is grammatical), so the blanket claim that -masu blocks every subordinate clause is false and will be contradicted by input within days. The channel split exists because the social-cost asymmetry is real: over-polite is at worst stiff, wrong-register plain is an offense. And the -masu shell is not four memorized endings — it is the i-stem plus five endings (-masu, -masen, -mashita, -masen deshita, -mashoo, plus -masen ka for invitations), and the i-stem is a key you need anyway.
laws.consequence: Cuts roughly 40% off the card count and makes a four-month grammar sprint arithmetically possible. It also relocates the naming of the i-stem to week 6-7, where it is free, converting twenty later 'grammar points' (-tai, -nagara, -ni iku, -kata, -sugiru, -yasui, -nikui, -hajimeru, -dasu, -owaru, -tsuzukeru, -naosu, -komu, -soo, -nasai, o-V-ni naru) into one morphological operation plus twenty tails.

laws.name: Contrast to define; separate to encode; frame when both
laws.statement: Items whose meaning IS the opposition must be co-taught inside one unit. Items that share a sound shape must be admitted one at a time behind a retrieval-strength gate. When an item is both, no spacing saves you — encode it in a frame whose particle supplies a non-phonological cue.
laws.mechanism: A one-member category has no boundary, so the learner fills it from L1: wa taught alone becomes 'the subject slot', and because bare wa is almost never ungrammatical in a main clause there is zero negative evidence, so every fluent-sounding sentence reinforces the wrong hypothesis for years. Conversely, two items sharing a phonological form with competing meanings is an A-B/A-C paired-associate list, the structure that maximizes retroactive interference, and for an ear-only learner the sound is the ENTIRE cue. The hard case is the -eru and -rareru families, where potential, transitive, passive, and honorific all wear one shape — kaeru (can buy) vs kaeru (change), kireru (is cut) vs kireru (can cut), yakeru, toreru, wareru, nukeru, and taberareru as passive / potential / honorific. Inflection does not separate these, because the potential of a godan verb is itself an ichidan verb with an identical -te form. The surviving cue is argument structure: potential takes ga, transitive takes o.
laws.consequence: wa/ga in one six-day unit at week 4, never wa alone. ageru/kureru/morau as one triangle. The two -te iru readings in one session. The four conditionals never all at once. Potential at week 13 and transitivity pairs at month 8, a minimum of five weeks apart, both carded in full frames with the particle. And accent does part of this work for free: kaeru [1] vs kaeru [0], kiru [1] vs kiru [0] are accent minimal pairs, so they are trained in the phonology block rather than deferred by months. Only the accent-identical collisions get the separation treatment — and note that atsui 'thick' is [0] while atsui 'hot' is [2], so it is a split, not a merge.

laws.name: Rules front-loaded, but never before their induction base
laws.statement: A multiplier enters as soon as ~40 applicable bases exist, presented with 12-15 attested types spanning varied bases before extension is licensed. This sets a floor, never a ceiling.
laws.mechanism: Morphological patterns become productive as a function of TYPE frequency, not token frequency: -sugiru heard on two verbs is two idioms, on fifteen it is a rule. The corollary bites hardest on the -te chant. The standard induction set (taberu, iku, suru, kuru) contains one ichidan verb, the two irregulars, and the single verb that violates the -ku > -ite rule — not one regular godan verb, so it cannot possibly teach -u/-tsu/-ru > -tte, -mu/-bu/-nu > -nde, -ku > -ite, -gu > -ide, -su > -shite. Separately, the popular model of multiplier value as a decaying asset is wrong: a rule learned at month 12 applies retroactively to everything already known. What you actually forfeit is roughly linear — the slots wasted memorizing instances one at a time, plus the encounters you failed to parse in the interim. Only the second term is unrecoverable.
laws.consequence: The grammar gate is an induction base, not a word count: >=500 recognized words including >=40 verbs already stored as (dictionary, -te) audio pairs with >=4 per godan coda class (kau/katte, matsu/matte, toru/totte, yomu/yonde, asobu/asonde, shinu/shinde, kaku/kaite, isogu/isoide, hanasu/hanashite), with iku kept OUT of the induction set and taught afterward as the sole exception. N+suru waits for 40 Sino-Japanese nouns and for an acoustic heuristic that identifies them by ear. The opaque compound tails (-komu, -kiru, -au, -naosu, -kakeru) are ~60 memorized items at month 10, not a rule, because they over-generate into forms nobody says and there is no negative evidence in the input.

laws.name: Closed sets sprint and retire on a test; open sets change source and never stop
laws.statement: Every closed set gets a measurable exit condition AND a hard calendar ceiling. Every open set switches supply rather than terminating.
laws.mechanism: Past roughly 90% comprehension of the core closed set, the remaining patterns are rare enough that their expected encounter rate in ordinary input exceeds any plausible drilling efficiency, so marginal return on explicit study goes to approximately zero. Syllabi have no terminal point — publishers do, which is why the N4-to-N3-to-N2 pattern-book regress consumes years. The hard ceiling exists because failing the exit test is usually evidence of a SPEED deficit, and more drilling cannot touch speed.
laws.consequence: Grammar terminates on a 140-item unseen audio battery at natural speed, >=90%, hard ceiling month 9, monthly re-test thereafter. But the closed set has to actually be closed: the conventional list omits adjective inflection (-kunai/-katta/-kute/-ku plus ii > yokatta), the volitional, the request and prohibition paradigm, obligation forms, comparison, question words including nande/dooshite, and the entire numeral-and-counter system. Vocabulary switches from frequency list to mining when the unknown-word rate in real material drops below ~15 per 10 minutes, and then runs forever.

laws.name: Review load is the schedule, and it obeys a different formula than everyone uses
laws.statement: Steady-state reviews per day is approximately 6-7 x new cards per day once the pipeline matures — NOT new-per-day times the sum of reciprocal intervals. Every N you choose is a permanent tax in minutes.
laws.mechanism: A card occupies interval step I_k for I_k days and generates exactly one review to leave it, so each step contributes N reviews/day once filled. The count of reviews is therefore the count of ladder steps reached, not the sum of their reciprocals. Sanity check: ladder {1 day, then 100 days}, N=1. The reciprocal model predicts about 1 review/day; after 1,000 days reality is about 10. Costing that at ~5 s per audio comprehension press, ~15 s per production press, production on ~40% of items, plus ~40 s same-day encoding per new card, gives roughly 2 minutes/day per new-card-per-day at maturity. All of these numbers are estimates, but the 3x error in the standard formula is not.
laws.consequence: N caps at 20/day, ramping 10 (weeks 3-4) to 15 (weeks 5-10) to 20 (week 11 onward). Six thousand recognized items lands at month 12-13, not month 9 — and roughly a quarter of them arrive free from multipliers (N+suru, the i-stem tails, o-/go- stripping, rendaku, the ka/mo/demo paradigm, morpheme families) rather than from cards, which is what makes the target reachable at all. The taper at month 12 is a CLIFF, not a glide: the short-interval steps carry almost all the cost and a glide keeps refilling them, so cutting to zero drops load 40-60% within 3-5 weeks and then trails.

laws.name: Coverage gates whether input is acquisition; latency gates whether it is comprehension
laws.statement: Below roughly 95% lemma coverage, input is decoration. Above it, the binding constraint stops being what you know and becomes how fast you retrieve it. The metric must switch at that point.
laws.mechanism: Incidental acquisition needs enough known context to make the unknown item inferable and to leave working memory free to notice it; below threshold you get guessing, which encodes wrong meanings that are hard to dislodge. But word counts are the wrong trigger, because two learners with identical decks can differ by 40 points on running speech. Japanese conversation runs at roughly 7-8 morae per second — 420-480 morae per minute, not the 250 that graded material uses — and lexical access must complete in a few hundred milliseconds or the parse falls behind and collapses. A flashcard gives you five seconds and rewards you for using them.
laws.consequence: Input ignition fires on a comprehension test at ~350 morae/min (news/announcer pace), not on a word count; the terminal phase steps to 450+ morae/min of unscripted multi-party speech, because that is where overlap, particle drop, and reduction actually live. Active input is capped at 20 min/day before ignition and uncapped after. From month 11 the metric is continuous shadowing lag under 1 second at 350+ morae/min, and card latency is measured from clip OFFSET, not onset. The hard rule: if listening comprehension does not improve for six consecutive weeks while vocabulary grows by 1,000+, halve new cards that week.

laws.name: Head-final parsing is capacity, not knowledge
laws.statement: Noun-modifying clauses, embedded questions, and the clause-final predicate complex respond to time-on-task, not to explanation. Budget them 3-5x what a textbook does and start exposure well before instruction.
laws.mechanism: English is head-initial and parsed incrementally: 'the book [that I bought]' lets you attach the head before the modifier arrives. Japanese is head-final — 'kinoo katta hon' forces the listener to hold an unresolved, complete-sounding predicate in working memory with no relative pronoun, no comma, and in speech no prosodic break, until the head noun arrives and retroactively assigns it a role. Worse, tense, negation, modality, evidentiality, and politeness all stack on the clause-final verb complex (tabenakatta n ja nai ka to omou), so the whole clause must be held open and resolved at the end. This is the dominant listening bottleneck for English speakers and the one place where audio-first is materially harder than reading-first, because the page supplies word boundaries and the option to re-read.
laws.consequence: Relative clauses get five days plus a permanent background track to the end of the program, and they PRECEDE nominalization and quotation — because [clause]+no, [clause]+koto, ka doo ka, and N to iu N are all the same prenominal parse, so the conventional order puts the dependent before its prerequisite. A truncation drill runs from week 9: hear a clause with the final predicate complex clipped, predict polarity and tense; then hear full clauses of increasing length and answer polarity/tense questions only.

laws.name: The card unit is whatever the ear can identify
laws.statement: Merge orthographic splits that are phonologically and accentually identical; split phonological near-pairs; and for the Sino-Japanese half of the lexicon, the card unit is a collocation, not a word.
laws.mechanism: A reader disambiguates kikan (period / institution / engine), kooen (park / lecture / support), shiritsu (private / municipal) by kanji. An ear-only learner has nothing. Kango is 2-morae-x-2 with heavy long vowels, geminates, and moraic N: low phonological distinctiveness and extreme homophone density — exactly the wrong profile. Conversely, three kanji spellings with one sound and one accent (atsui 'weather-hot' and atsui 'touch-hot', both [2]) are literally one signal, and making separate cards produces identical prompts, which is unlearnable by construction and becomes a permanent leech. Wago is the opposite profile: longer, more varied CV shapes, low homophone density, cheap by ear.
laws.consequence: Wago cards are bare audio; kango cards carry a 2-4 mora frame from the start (kikan ga nagai / kikan ni tsutomeru), which costs ~2 s more per press and is priced into the N=20 cap. The wago:kango ratio runs ~85:15 through the first 1,000 items and flips to ~40:60 by 6,000. An acoustic heuristic for identifying Sino roots by ear (1-2 morae, ends in a vowel or -N/-tsu/-ku/-ki, takes long vowels and geminates freely, never inflects, occurs bare in compounds) is drilled as a classification task before N+suru is licensed, since three separate multipliers are otherwise gated on a distinction the learner cannot make.

stages.title: Pipeline validation and the notation contract
stages.trigger: Program start. No prerequisites.
stages.phonology: Validate the TTS pipeline against an accent reference (OJAD/NHK) on a 200-item sample; check that geminate and long-vowel duration ratios survive synthesis and that devoicing is rendered, not deleted. Swap or tune voices until agreement is >=95%. Fix the notation contract, used on card BACKS only: one dot-separated slot per mora, long vowels always doubled, moraic nasal as capital N in its own slot, sokuon as capital Q in its own slot, palatal digraph inside one slot, devoiced vowels parenthesized, accent number plus H/L string, integer beat count appended. to-o-kyo-o [0] LHHH (4). ga-Q-ko-o [0] (4). shi-N-bu-N [0] (4). de-sh(i)-ta (3 beats, 2 voiced). Absolute rule: romaji is never read aloud; every utterance is an echo of audio.
stages.vocab: Zero. No cards exist yet.
stages.grammar: Zero.
stages.output: 60-item two-alternative forced-choice baseline pretest across long vowels, geminates, moraic N, and 2-mora accent in the -ga frame. A nontrivial minority of adults are above chance on length on day one; the result reweights the time budget of stages 1-2 but removes no unit.
stages.why: Everything downstream is scored in beats and tagged with accent. If the TTS is accent-unreliable — and most Japanese TTS is — the accent tags are unverifiable and the whole card format is built on sand. Two days is the cheapest insurance in the program.
stages.exitTest: TTS agrees with the accent reference on >=95% of a 200-item sample; baseline forced-choice scores recorded per contrast.
stages.dailyBraid: 45 min pipeline check, 30 min notation drill (write and verify beat counts for 40 heard words), 15 min baseline test.

stages.title: The mora grid: isochrony, pure vowels, pitch decoupled from stress
stages.trigger: Stage 0 exit.
stages.phonology: (1) Equal-beat tapping on all-CV words containing NO special morae: ne-ko, i-nu, sa-ka-na, ta-ma-go, ko-ko-ro, o-to-ko, ku-da-mo-no, to-mo-da-chi, mu-ra-sa-ki. One finger strike per mora against a 60-90 bpm metronome. (2) Five pure monophthongs: kill schwa reduction and the English offglides on /e/ ([ei]) and /o/ ([ou]). Reduction is the more expensive of the two because it IS the mechanism by which ta-ma-go becomes 'tuh-MAH-goh'. (3) Pitch-is-not-stress decoupling: produce sa-ku-ra as LHH, HLL, LHL at constant loudness and constant mora duration. English bundles pitch, loudness, duration, and vowel quality into one 'stress' package; until that bundle is broken the learner cannot produce heiban and hears every accent drop as emphasis. (4) Loanword mora arithmetic as a self-checking corpus: su-to-ra-i-ku (5), ma-ku-do-na-ru-do (6), ko-N-pyu-u-ta-a (6), a-i-su-ku-ri-i-mu (7), sa-N-do-i-Q-chi (6), ko-o-hi-i (4), po-ke-Q-to (4), pa-N (2). (5) The r-tap, 30 minutes: it IS the t in 'water', the d in 'ladder' — never 'between l and d'. Intervocalic first (a-ri-ga-to-o, sa-ku-ra, ko-re), word-initial last with a vowel scaffold (a-raku > raku). Discriminate against /d/, not /l/. (6) ts via 'cats minus ca'; su/tsu discrimination (su-ki / tsu-ki, su-na / tsu-na). fu and hi named for LISTENING only, no drill — neither has a native contrast partner and English substitutions cost zero comprehension.
stages.vocab: Zero cards. Loanwords carry zero semantic load, which is exactly why they are the timing corpus.
stages.grammar: Zero.
stages.output: Echo repetition from day 1 (hear, one-second gap, reproduce, tapping beats) on 1-3 mora units and loanwords. Twelve seed chunks ordered by PHONOLOGICAL difficulty, not by social utility: hai, un, ee, soo, chigau, sumimasen, arigatoo first; the long polite formulas (yoroshiku onegaishimasu, otsukaresama desu, shitsurei shimasu) held to week 2 because they require devoicing and mora timing the learner does not yet have. Chorusing in unison from day 4 on material heard 5+ times. NO true lag shadowing yet.
stages.why: Length is a RATIO judgment and a ratio needs a stable denominator. If the neighbouring morae are being squeezed and schwa-reduced by English stress-timing, the contrast is not learnable — the learner passes two-alternative tests by attending to total word duration and then fails the moment words get longer. The r-tap is scheduled here despite ranking only eighth in fossilization damage, purely on cost: American English already contains the sound, so it is a relabelling exercise, and leaving an English retroflex in place r-colours the following vowel and quietly undoes the vowel-purity work.
stages.exitTest: 4-mora all-CV words produced with under ~20% inter-mora duration variance on a waveform; correct integer beat count on 20/20 unheard loanwords; sa-ku-ra produced in three pitch patterns with duration held flat.
stages.dailyBraid: 20 min tapping/isochrony, 15 min vowel purity, 20 min loanword beat counting, 20 min echo shadowing of seed chunks, 10 min pitch decoupling, 5 min r-tap (days 5-7).

stages.title: The three length contrasts, the accent system, devoicing last
stages.trigger: Stage 1 isochrony at criterion. Length work may begin at 75% on tapping — length and gemination share a perceptual substrate and train better overlapping.
stages.phonology: Long vowels in three tiers by cue size: A word-final, /o/ and /a/ (e / ee, i-e / i-i-e, sa-to / sa-to-o, ka-do / ka-a-do); B word-medial, high vowels (o-ba-sa-N / o-ba-a-sa-N, o-ji-sa-N / o-ji-i-sa-N, yu-ki / yu-u-ki, shu-ji-N / shu-u-ji-N); C low-prominence position and stacked special morae (ko-o-ko-o-se-e (5) vs ko-ko-se (3), byo-o-ki (3) vs bi-yo-ki). Moraic N as a full beat with controlled pairs where only the beat count differs: ta-ni / ta-N-i, ki-ne-N / ki-N-e-N, a-na-i / a-N-na-i, te-N-i-N (4). N assimilation ([shimbuN], [sampo], [riNgo]) is LISTENING ONLY, 20 minutes, no production drill — it is coarticulatory and free once the beat is held. Sokuon inverted from every textbook: FRICATIVE geminates first (i-sho / i-Q-sho, za-Q-shi, ki-Q-sa-te-N) because the cue is audible friction, then STOP geminates (ki-te / ki-Q-te, ma-ta / ma-Q-ta, sa-ka / sa-Q-ka) where the cue is a beat of SILENCE and English has no phonemic silence-length. Hook: English cross-word gemination in 'black cat', 'hot tub'. Palatal morae are ONE beat: kyo-o (2) / ki-yo-o (3), ju-u (2) / ji-yu-u (3), byo-o-i-N (4) / bi-yo-o-i-N (5). Rate and talker sweep from day 4: every pair at 0.75x / 1.0x / 1.3x across 6+ voices, isolated AND in two carrier frames ('___ desu ka', '___ o kudasai'). ACCENT: the two invariants (pitch drops at most once per word; morae 1 and 2 always differ), the four classes, and the -ga frame — ha-na ga LHH (nose, heiban) vs ha-na ga LHL (flower, odaka), ha-shi ga in three patterns, a-me [1]/[0], ka-ki [1]/[0], plus the interference set that accent RELEASES: kaeru [1] return / kaeru [0] change, kiru [1] cut / kiru [0] wear, atsui [2] hot / atsui [0] thick, omoi [0] heavy / omoi [2] thought. DEVOICING LAST, days 11-13: desu > [des] but still 2 beats, deshita > [deshta] but still 3, gakusee > [gaksee] but still 4, -masu on every polite verb. Perception only; no devoiced production drilled here.
stages.vocab: Still zero cards.
stages.grammar: Zero.
stages.output: Chorusing continues. True lag shadowing (~0.5 s) begins day 9 and ONLY on material the learner can already beat-count. Standing rule for the next 24 months: never shadow what you cannot beat-count.
stages.why: Fricative-before-stop gemination is the one inversion that saves a demoralizing day-5 wall: establish 'this consonant is worth an extra beat' on a positive cue, then transfer to a negative one. Devoicing is placed last for the reason nearly every course gets backwards — devoicing removes VOICING, not TIME, and told on day 1 that 'desu is really des', an English speaker deletes the mora too, because English has no representation for a beat with no voiced nucleus. The beat grid must be automatic before it has to survive the loss of the acoustic cue. Accent enters here, not later, because heiban and odaka are indistinguishable on the bare word: the 'X ga' recording convention must be fixed before card 1 or the entire deck needs re-recording.
stages.exitTest: TIERED, 4-week ceiling. Primary: >=85% on 60 unseen minimal-pair items across 3 unheard voices at 3 rates, isolated and in carrier frames. Gate drill: kite / kiite / kitte at >=90% on 40 three-alternative trials. 75-85% releases card 1 with a mandatory 10 min/day continuing discrimination track through month 3; below 75% at 4 weeks releases anyway with the continuing track and monthly re-test.
stages.dailyBraid: 25 min length tiers, 20 min gemination/moraic N, 15 min rate-talker sweep, 15 min accent in the -ga frame, 15 min shadowing (echo > chorus > lag).

stages.title: Particle-free predicate core, kosoado, and the bootstrapping toolkit
stages.trigger: Stage 2 exit (any tier). Vocabulary opens at 10 new cards/day.
stages.phonology: Continuing discrimination track 10 min/day for any contrast below 85%. Every new card carries its accent number and beat count; every noun is recorded with -ga. Downstream drill begins: mark where the pitch drops in a 10-second clip and count accentual phrases.
stages.vocab: ~280 items at 10/day. Response tokens and aizuchi, which sit in the top 20 of any conversational corpus and outside the top 3000 of any written one: un, uun (the highest-frequency minimal pair in the language — yes vs no by length and contour alone), hai, iie, ee, aa, hee, soo, naruhodo, sokka, honto?, majide, tashika ni. Social chunks unanalyzed: arigatoo, sumimasen, gomen, ohayoo, konnichiwa, oyasumi, jaa ne, daijoobu, yokatta, chotto matte, otsukaresama, yoroshiku onegaishimasu (whole-string frequency vastly exceeds the product of its parts; negau is around rank 4000). Kosoado as a clean 4x5 grid (20 cells, 3 exceptions flagged): kore/sore/are/dore, kono/sono/ano/dono, koko/soko/asoko (suppletive), konna/sonna/anna/donna, koo/soo/aa/doo. Kochira-series and -itsu held one week as an appended column. Question inventory INCLUDING nande and dooshite. ~180 concrete high-frequency nouns, randomized by conversational frequency rank, never thematically grouped.
stages.grammar: Not a sprint — these are lexicon-like closed frames that make vocabulary utterable. Copula: da / desu / ja nai / datta / deshita / ja nakatta (de wa nai is recognition only). N no N. Topic wa deliberately withheld until stage 4. Final particles ne, yo, yo ne, na, kke, sa, no(rising) taught prosodically, not semantically. Rising terminal intonation IS the plain-speech question marker; ka is marked as the polite variant. The so-/a- split stated correctly: a- = referent both parties know from direct experience; so- = referent known from the discourse only, regardless of who introduced it ('Kinoo eiga o mita. Sore wa yokatta'). n da / n desu / n ja nai? / n da kedo admitted here as a FROZEN sentence-final pattern with a scheduled unpack at stage 15 — its internal structure is invisible to a listener anyway and it appears in roughly a fifth of spontaneous utterances.
stages.output: The bootstrapping kit, at item ~30 and ahead of most content vocabulary because it changes the shape of the curve rather than a point on it: 'X tte nani?', 'doo iu imi?', 'moo ichido onegaishimasu', 'yukkuri onegaishimasu', 'nan te itta?', 'nihongo de nan te iimasu ka', 'kore de ii?', 'chigau / chigau yo'. Passive uncomprehended listening starts here, off-clock, unlimited, for prosody and segmentation only. Active listening capped at 12 min/day on scripted dialogue.
stages.why: Unit 1 and 2 of the vocabulary track are deliberately particle-free — not as a simplification but because casual Japanese drops wa, ga, and especially o at high rates, so particle-free utterances are the dominant form in the input. Training on the elliptical form first makes the fully-marked form trivially parseable later; the reverse is not true, because a parser that expects particles as segmentation cues receives 'nani tabeta?' as an unsegmentable blur. Kosoado goes in whole because the grid factors (4 morphemes x 5 endings = 9 things, not 20) and because the anaphoric so/a split is invisible if the rows are drip-fed — drip-fed learners spend years believing a- means 'far away' and never use ano hito for a mutual acquaintance.
stages.exitTest: Extracts 10 unknown nouns from a scripted TTS interlocutor using only the bootstrapping frames, no English. Kosoado grid 20/20 by ear. Recognizes rising-intonation questions with no ka at >=90%. ~280 cards at >=90% retention.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow warmup, 20 min new cards, 15 min review, 15 min kosoado/aizuchi drill, 10 min continuing discrimination, 15 min active listening. Passive listening off-clock.

stages.title: Existence, wa vs ga as one indivisible contrast, the ga-marked-object class
stages.trigger: Stage 3 exit. ~280 recognized words.
stages.phonology: Continuing track. Accentual-phrase downstep noticing extends to 20-second clips.
stages.vocab: To ~500 at 10-15/day. aru/iru/nai/inai/atta/ita. Relational nouns: ue, shita, naka, soto, mae, ushiro, tonari, yoko, aida, chikaku, migi, hidari. Place nouns: ie, uchi, mise, eki, gakkoo, kaisha, heya, toire, kooen. The ga-marked-object predicates, which most curricula scatter: suki, kirai, daisuki, joozu, heta, hoshii, wakaru, dekiru. Family terms as a closed in-group/out-group oppositional set taught row-complete: otoosan/chichi, okaasan/haha, oniisan/ani, oneesan/ane, otooto, imooto. Receptive pronoun set: ore, omae, kimi, uchi, atashi, with the gendering noted. anata is DELETED from the curriculum; the address slot is name+san.
stages.grammar: wa and ga in ONE six-day unit, never wa alone. Diagnostic taught operationally, not glossed: a question word never takes wa and its answer takes ga (Dare ga kita? — Tanaka-san ga); what is already in play takes wa. ni-1 (location of existence) introduced against de-1 (locus of action) in the same session: kooen ni iru / kooen de asobu, uchi ni aru / uchi de taberu. mo as substitution for wa/ga/o. Contrastive wa (biiru wa nomu kedo, wain wa nomanai). Double-nominative (zoo wa hana ga nagai, atama ga itai). Explicit PARTICLE-DROP drill: the same sentence with and without ga/o, with the elliptical version as the production target — in the existential frame the only possible particle is ga, and the particle is frequently absent ('koko ni aru yo', 'toire doko?').
stages.output: Active listening 15 min/day. Production limited to copula frames and existence in the -masu shell (arimasu / imasu / arimasen).
stages.why: The single highest-stakes decision in the plan. Taught alone, wa is defined by the learner as the subject slot, because that is the only hypothesis L1 makes available and bare wa is almost never ungrammatical in a main clause — so there is zero negative evidence and thousands of fluent-sounding sentences reinforce the error. It makes zoo wa hana ga nagai, nihongo ga wakaru, and sushi ga suki unparseable, and unlearning is overwriting rather than filling. Introducing ga inside the existential frame is what makes a 15-item gap possible: it is the frame where ga is the only possible particle and wa is odd, so the contrast is demonstrable rather than asserted. iru (need) is NOT taught here despite the frequency — it collides with iru (exist) and waits 8 weeks.
stages.exitTest: >=18/20 on a wa/ga forced-choice audio battery including wh-answers, contrastive wa, double-nominative sentences, and 5 particle-dropped items; ni/de contrast >=18/20.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 20 min new, 20 min review, 20 min wa/ga minimal-pair drill, 10 min continuing discrimination, 15 min active listening.

stages.title: Numbers, counters, dates, times, and the transaction script
stages.window: Weeks 5-8, running parallel to stages 4 and 6
stages.trigger: Stage 2 exit. Gated on the mora grid, not on grammar — the counter sound changes ARE the special-mora contrasts already trained.
stages.phonology: The counter alternations drilled as CHANTS, not tables: obstruent-triggered gemination and nasal-triggered voicing, conditioned left-to-right (not 'rendaku', which is a different process, and not 'regressive'). ippon / nihon / sanbon / yonhon / gohon / roppon / nanahon / happon, nanbon. ippun / nifun / sanpun / yonpun / gofun / roppun / nanafun / happun / juppun, nanpun. ikkai / nikai / sangai / rokkai / hakkai / jukkai, nangai.
stages.vocab: To ~700. 1-99; hyaku, sanbyaku, roppyaku, happyaku; sen, hassen; ichiman (the base-10000 break that makes it not juusen). The wago -tsu series in full, hitotsu through too (NOT 'tokoo') plus ikutsu — this is the escape hatch that makes the counter tail safely droppable. hitori / futari / sannin / nannin. The yon/shi, nana/shichi, kyuu/ku alternations with their lexicalized exceptions: yoji not yonji, kuji not kyuuji, shichiji not nanaji. Ten counters at cells 1-6 plus nan- only (~56 items, not 300): -nin, -ko, -mai, -hon, -hiki, -dai, -kai(times), -kai/-gai(floor), -hai, -sai (issai, nisai, hatachi, nansai). Cells 7-10 are never rehearsed. Date readings as pure rote, the highest-value non-derivable set in the numeric track: tsuitachi, futsuka, mikka, yokka, itsuka, muika, nanoka, yooka, kokonoka, tooka, juuyokka, hatsuka. Times, -jikan, -yoobi, kyoo/ashita/asatte/kinoo/ototoi, konshuu/raishuu/senshuu, mainichi. gurai (quantity) vs goro (time point). Quantifier float: biiru o nihon nomu vs nihon no biiru.
stages.grammar: ni with absolute time (sanji ni, getsuyoobi ni) vs bare relative time (ashita, kinoo) — the rule is calendrical-vs-deictic, not arbitrary. kara / made / made ni.
stages.output: The RECEPTIVE service-encounter script installed here as unanalyzed audio, ~15 items, roughly 1400 items earlier than any standard plan puts keigo: irasshaimase, X-en ni narimasu, fukuro go-riyoo desu ka, atatamemasu ka, shooshoo omachi kudasai, go-chuumon wa o-kimari desu ka, kochira de yoroshii deshoo ka. Production frames: 'N onegaishimasu', 'N kudasai', 'ikura desu ka' — taught as frozen lexical items since o and the -masu shell do not exist yet.
stages.why: Absent from three of the five source analyses and the largest single omission in all of them. Counters are a closed set saturated with irregular sound changes that exist ONLY in speech, they are unavoidable in every transaction, and they are needed before conversation onset at month 4. Mishearing a number costs money; using the wrong counter costs a mild oddity — so numbers get full memorization, the counter tail gets none, and the -tsu series covers the residue. The keigo split is decided by the same logic that governs everything else: if service-encounter comprehension is mandatory from week one, then by the objective function it belongs near the front of the RECEPTIVE queue, while productive keigo morphology belongs at the very back.
stages.exitTest: Audio dictation of 30 quantities, times, and dates under a 2-second deadline at >=90%, including all four irregular date readings and the yoji/kuji/shichiji exceptions.
stages.dailyBraid: Folded into stages 4 and 6: 15 min/day of counter and date chanting, replacing the continuing-discrimination slot on days when that is at criterion.

stages.title: Keys 1 and 3: dictionary form, verb classes, the i-stem named, the -masu shell, core particles
stages.trigger: THE GRAMMAR GATE, stated as an induction base rather than a word count: >=500 recognized words, >=150 chunks, and >=40 verbs already stored as (dictionary, -te) audio pairs including >=4 per godan coda class.
stages.phonology: Verb accent class tagged on every card from here: accented verbs take the drop on the penultimate mora, shifting one left off a special mora (kaeru [1], hairu [1]); -masu forms are uniformly accented on 'ma' without exception.
stages.vocab: To ~800 at 15/day. First 60 verbs by conversational frequency, with suru and iu present from the start (suru outranks aru and iru in every frequency list, contrary to a claim in one source analysis). The -eru/-iru trap set: kaeru(return), hairu, hashiru, shiru, kiru(cut), iru(need — now admitted, 8 weeks after iru 'exist'), shaberu, kagiru. These are admitted here rather than deferred because they are ACCENT-distinguished from their homophones and the stage-2 work released them.
stages.grammar: Key 1: dictionary form as the comprehension citation form; non-past covers habitual and future. Two classes plus suru/kuru. Lexical pairing rule — every verb stored as (dictionary, -te), class never computed, one extra syllable of storage buying the elimination of a rule, a diagnostic, and an exception list. Key 3 named HERE rather than at its conventional late position: the i-stem (nomi-, tabe-, machi-, hanashi-, shi-, ki-), with the tsu > chi and su > shi palatalizations stated explicitly, because the -masu shell needs a stem column the learner has never met. The shell: -masu / -masen / -mashita / -masen deshita / -mashoo / -masen ka (invitation — not derivable and omitted from every four-item list). Particles for SPEECH: wa, ga, o, ni, de, to, no, mo, kara, made, made ni, toka. o-2 taught here alongside o-1: path and departure with intransitive motion verbs (michi o aruku, ie o deru, basu o oriru, kooen o sanpo suru), against ni (goal: eki ni tsuku) and de (locus: koko de aruku). noru takes ni and oriru takes o, flagged as frame-bound idiosyncrasy memorized with the verb.
stages.output: Production switches to the -masu shell for all sentence-final predication. Active listening 15 min/day. Grammar drills are audio transformation under a 2-second deadline — hear taberu, say tabemasu — because an untimed conjugation drill trains a lookup habit that fails at 7 morae/second.
stages.why: The gate is an induction base because a rule with no stored exemplars has nothing to generalize over, and the conventional 800-word gate measures the wrong thing. Naming the i-stem HERE, where it is free (the learner is learning -masu anyway), converts twenty later 'grammar points' into one morphological operation plus twenty tails, and it repairs the standard plan's hidden defect: -masu attaches to a stem column the learner otherwise never meets. o-2 is included because every plan that teaches o as 'the object particle' and then teaches aruku, deru, and oriru produces *ie kara deru and *michi de aruku, and worse, mis-parses the heard forms.
stages.exitTest: Class assignment by ear for 40 unheard verbs under 2 s at >=95%; -masu shell produced for 30 verbs; ni/de/o three-way selection >=18/20 including three path-o items.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 15 min new, 25 min review, 20 min timed grammar drill, 15 min active listening, 10 min counter chant.

stages.title: Key 2: the -nai stem
stages.trigger: Stage 6 exit — class assignment must be automatic, because -nai is where the classes diverge most audibly.
stages.phonology: Accent on -nai forms folded into the chant rather than left for a later pass.
stages.vocab: To ~900 at 15/day.
stages.grammar: -nai formation. Ru-verbs drop -ru. U-verbs take -a-nai. The w-insertion rule stated CORRECTLY and in the only notation the learner has: any verb whose dictionary form ends in a vowel plus u — -au, -iu, -ou, -uu — takes -wanai. kau/kawanai, IU/IWANAI, omou/omowanai, suu/suwanai. The conventional statement omits -iu and therefore mis-generates for iu, which is among the highest-frequency verbs in speech and is the source of -tte, the item this plan leans on hardest at stage 15. suru > shinai, kuru > konai, aru > nai (suppletive). -nakatta. -nakute (causal/state linking) vs -naide (manner/without) — the pair textbooks blur into one. -naide kudasai. -n contraction (wakaran, shiran, ikan) recognition only. mada + NEG vs moo + affirmative introduced as a 2x2 grid, not a two-item pair: mou tabeta / mou nai / mada tabete inai (note the -te form requirement, which is invisible without the grid and produces *mada tabemasen) / mada aru.
stages.output: Both non-past polarities produced under a 2-second deadline. Active listening 15 min.
stages.why: -nai comes before -te, against the instinct to rush the hinge node, for two reasons. It exposes the a-stem that passive and causative will attach to at month 8, so this unit quietly lays a second foundation. And it means the learner enters the -te chant with both polarities automatic, so the chant is drilled on a full lexicon rather than half of one.
stages.exitTest: -nai and -nakatta for 40 unheard verbs under 2 s at >=95%, with iwanai and kawanai among them; mada/mou 2x2 all four cells produced correctly.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 15 min new, 25 min review, 20 min timed -nai chant, 15 min active listening, 10 min truncation drill (predict the clipped clause-final complex).

stages.title: Key 4: the -te chant, and -ta free with it
stages.trigger: Stage 7 exit. The largest single time budget in the course.
stages.phonology: The chant IS the phonology: nasal-triggered voicing and obstruent-triggered gemination, the same processes trained in stage 2 and chanted in stage 5's counters. Assimilation minimal pairs at ceiling: kite (kuru) / kite (kiru, wear) / kitte (kiru, cut). Accent contour drilled as part of the chant, never accent-blind.
stages.vocab: To ~1,050. Verb intake continues at ~30% of new cards.
stages.grammar: The full FIVE-way rule, stated completely because this is the only place it is ever stated: -u/-tsu/-ru > -tte (katte, matte, totte); -mu/-bu/-nu > -nde (nonde, shinde, asonde); -ku > -ite (kaite); -gu > -IDE (oyoide, isoide); -su > -SHITE (hanashite); ru-verbs > -te; suru > shite; kuru > kite. Then iku > itte taught SEPARATELY as the sole exception, and kept out of the induction set entirely so it cannot teach the wrong generalization for the -ku class. -ta is the SAME slot with the final vowel swapped e > a — voicing is already fixed by the stem and is identical in both paradigms (nonde/nonda, kaite/kaita, shite/shita). One chant, two full paradigms. HOMOPHONE LEDGER entries opened here, since the -te form is elsewhere used as a disambiguator and here it is the collision: kite has three owners (kuru, kiru-wear, and kitte from kiru-cut), and itte has two (iku, iu) that inflection does NOT separate — disambiguate by frame (fuku o kite / uchi ni kite / kami o kitte; eki ni itte / 'X' tte itte). -te sequencing with tense carried only by the final verb. -te causal. Bare -te as casual request (tabete, matte, kiite, yamete) as the production target; -te kudasai marked explicitly as a frozen politeness chunk with a scheduled unpack.
stages.output: Production speed is the whole point: the -te form of any verb must come out in under 300 ms, because roughly 35 constructions are about to be built on it and any latency compounds 35 ways. Active listening 18 min.
stages.why: The hinge. Standard curricula place this at Genki ch. 6 or Minna L14, roughly month 3; here it is week 9 — later than the pure dependency graph would put it (day 22) because a validated ear and a real induction base come first, and far earlier than a textbook because 45 constructions are waiting. This is also where audio-first is at maximum advantage: the alternations are assimilation, they are a rhythm, and they drill as a song. A reading-first learner meets them as a five-row table keyed to kana columns and gets no motor program out of it.
stages.exitTest: -te and -ta produced for any of 80 unheard verbs in under 300 ms at >=95%; kite/kitte/itte disambiguated by frame in a 20-item audio battery at >=85%.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 15 min new, 25 min review, 25 min -te chant to speed, 15 min active listening.

stages.title: -teru and the aspect cluster
stages.trigger: Stage 8 exit.
stages.phonology: -teta (SHORT vowel, 3 morae, produced by deletion of the /i/ with no compensatory lengthening) vs -tetta (geminate, 4 morae): futteta / futtetta, motteta / mottetta. A mora-count contrast carrying an aspect-vs-motion distinction, invisible to a reader and brutal to a listener.
stages.vocab: To ~1,200. Change-of-state verbs carded WITH their -teru meaning, because the resultative reading is lexical.
stages.grammar: -teru is the citation form; -te iru is the careful/formal variant; -temasu is the polite form (the /i/ drops even in polite speech). -tenai / -teta / -tenakatta / -teru no? / -ten no?. The TWO cells co-taught in one session and keyed on aktionsart, never sequentially: durative verb > progressive (tabeteru, hanashiteru, matteru); punctual or change-of-state verb > resultant state (shitteru, motteru, sunderu, kekkon shiteru, shinderu, kiteru = is wearing, tsukareteru, niteru, aiteru). shitteru's negative is SHIRANAI, suppletive, not *shitte inai — the most common single error in the class and absent from every source analysis's item list. -te iku > -teku (motteku, tsureteku). The three-way tokoro: -ru tokoro (about to) / -teru tokoro (in the middle of) / -ta tokoro (just did).
stages.output: Active listening 20 min. Aizuchi drill begins, 5 min/day: not clock-timed but CUE-triggered — respond at clause-final particles (ne, kedo, kara, de), at pauses, and at terminal contours, graded on landing within ~300 ms of a juncture. A stopwatch drill teaches the learner to interrupt mid-clause, which is worse than silence.
stages.why: -teru is the most frequent verb inflection in conversational Japanese after the plain non-past and -ta, so it takes the first slot in the -te fan-out — this is not a close call. Teaching it as 'the present progressive' is the second most expensive misconception in Japanese after wa-as-subject: shinde iru gets heard as 'is dying', shitte iru as 'is knowing', kite iru as 'is coming', and the English gloss is plausible enough to survive for years with no error signal. And the contracted form is primary because the deferred -teru of the standard plan means three months drilling a form the learner will rarely hear while the form they hear constantly is withheld.
stages.exitTest: 20/20 assigning progressive vs resultant reading by verb class; -teta/-tetta discrimination >=18/20; shiranai produced correctly in 5/5 elicited negatives.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 15 min new, 28 min review, 18 min aspect drill, 5 min aizuchi, 20 min active listening.

stages.title: Adjective inflection: the -ku core and the two classes
stages.trigger: Stage 9 exit. Pulled forward from its fanout-ranked position because four later nodes require it and every standard plan silently violates its own dependency graph by using -kunai and -ku naru before teaching them.
stages.phonology: Adjective accent class tagged (takai [2], samui [2], ookii [3]; akai [0], amai [0], karui [0]).
stages.vocab: To ~1,400. ~60 core adjectives, randomized. The three atsui MERGED where accent is identical (atsui 'weather-hot' and atsui 'touch-hot', both [2], are literally one signal and separate cards produce identical prompts) but atsui 'thick' [0] SPLIT, since it is accentually distinct. Same treatment for omoi [0] heavy vs omoi [2] thought.
stages.grammar: i-adjectives: attributive equals predicative, no copula. -kunai / -katta / -kunakatta / -kute / -ku. ii > yoku / yokatta / yokunai as full suppletion, drilled separately because yokatta alone is a top-30 spoken utterance. -ku naru / -ku suru. i-adj + desu adds politeness without inflecting (takakatta desu, never *takai deshita). na-adjectives ARE the copula paradigm from week 3, so they cost nothing: kirei da / kirei na / kirei ni / kirei de / kirei ja nai. Class assignment stated as a POSITIVE rule rather than a memorized trap list: an adjective ending in a vowel plus i — -ai, -ii, -ui, -oi — is an i-adjective; everything else is a na-adjective. This is the audio-first correction to a reading artifact: kirei is heard as /kiree/, teinei and yuumei end in /ee/, and genki ends in consonant-plus-i, so none of them is a lookalike by ear. The real exception list is about three: kirai, yukai (short u — yuukai with a long vowel is 'kidnapping'), and borrowed -i nouns. -ni naru / -ni suru. The three-way change-of-state set as one contrastive block: -ku naru (i-adj) / -ni naru (na-adj and N) / -yoo ni naru (verb, previewed).
stages.output: Evaluative statements in the -masu shell. Retell drill introduced: hear 45 seconds, reproduce the content aloud within 60 seconds of the clip ending, exploiting the priming window.
stages.why: The DAG correctly ranks adjective inflection below the -te subtree — fanout ~8 with no subtree beneath it — but its own sequence uses -te hoshikunai and samuku natte kita weeks earlier, which is a dependency violation, not a scheduling choice. Splitting the unit resolves it: the -ku/-kunai/-katta core lands here, where four downstream nodes need it, and the low-fanout remainder (comparison, degree adverbs, hodo/kurai) is deferred to month 7. The frozen-form mitigation from stage 3 (yokatta, oishikatta, takakatta, samukatta, sugoi, kawaii, yabai stored as vocabulary since week 3) means the paradigm arrives already sounding familiar and collapses to two days of morphology plus two of drilling.
stages.exitTest: 40 adjectives inflected in all four cells under 2 s; class assignment by ear 20/20 with no exception list consulted; yokatta/yokunai produced without *iikatta.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 15 min new, 28 min review, 18 min adjective drill, 5 min aizuchi, 20 min active listening.

stages.title: Key 5: potential, early and calibrated by stem length
stages.trigger: Stage 10 exit. Moved forward roughly six weeks from its conventional position and DELIBERATELY separated from the transitivity-pair stage by five weeks.
stages.phonology: Potential verbs are themselves ichidan verbs and re-enter the whole inflection system; accent tagged accordingly.
stages.vocab: To ~1,600 at 20/day (the cap).
stages.grammar: Godan -eru: nomeru, ikeru, hanaseru, yomeru, kaeru (can buy). Ichidan and kuru, calibrated rather than adopted wholesale: ra-nuki (tabereru, mireru, koreru, dereru) for 1-2 mora stems, where it is at or above parity in casual speech; -rareru for 3+ mora stems (oshierareru, kangaerareru, oboerareru), where ra-nuki is markedly rare and stigmatized and the learner will simply not hear *oshiereru. dekiru. The lexical pair mieru/kikoeru (spontaneous perception, no agent) vs mireru/kikeru (ability or opportunity) — a distinction English does not mark, so it goes unnoticed unless co-taught. Potential triggers o > ga (nihongo ga hanaseru), which is the third independent reinforcement of the ga-object class from stage 4. -tai / -takunai / -takatta as an i-stem tail inflecting as an i-adjective, with the o~ga alternation. THE ORDERING CONSTRAINT, stated explicitly on the card: the -eru potential of a godan verb is homophonous with the -eru transitive member of a transitivity pair — kaeru (can buy) vs kaeru (change), kireru (is cut) vs kireru (can cut), and the same for yakeru, toreru, wareru, nukeru. Inflection does not separate them; only argument structure does. Potential takes ga, transitive takes o. Both are therefore carded in full frames with the particle, never as bare verbs.
stages.output: Ability and inability statements. Conversation preparation: 30-second self-introduction rehearsed and recorded weekly. Active listening 22 min at 300 morae/min.
stages.why: This resolves the sharpest conflict between the source analyses. The dependency graph bundles potential with -eba at week 14 on the tidy grounds that both use the e-stem — which is exactly the pedagogical-symmetry tiebreak that fanout-weighting rejects everywhere else, and it chains a top-tier conversational function to a narrow one. The interference analysis moves potential early but schedules transitivity pairs one week before it, which is the tightest homophone collision anywhere in that plan. The synthesis takes potential early AND pushes transitivity to month 8, giving a five-week separation and letting argument structure carry the disambiguation the ear cannot.
stages.exitTest: Potential produced for 50 unheard verbs under 2 s; ga-marking correct in >=18/20; mieru vs mireru 10/10; ra-nuki applied only to short stems.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 12 min new, 30 min review, 18 min potential drill, 5 min aizuchi, 22 min active listening.

stages.title: -tara alone, obligation and permission, volitional, the request paradigm
stages.trigger: Stage 11 exit.
stages.phonology: Continuing accent tagging; devoicing now drilled in PRODUCTION on -masu forms (ikimas, tabemas) since the beat grid has been stable for three months.
stages.vocab: To ~2,000. dake, gurai/kurai, toka admitted here — toka is the default casual listing particle and outranks exhaustive to in conversation.
stages.grammar: -ta's dependents, since -ta itself cost nothing at stage 8: -ta koto ga aru / nai (experiential — promised and then omitted in one source analysis); -TARA as the conversational default conditional, taught ALONE and given six weeks to become the unmarked default; -tara doo?; -tari...-tari suru; -ta bakari; -ta hoo ga ii / -nai hoo ga ii. Temporal ordering triple: -ta ato de / -TE kara (time-since AND sequence: 'Nihon ni kite kara sannen' — the conventional label '-ta kara' is a different construction, the causal kara, and the mislabel is actively confusing) / [dictionary] mae ni, which takes non-past regardless of actual tense. Permission and obligation: -te mo ii, -te mo kamawanai, -cha dame / -cha ikenai (contraction primary), -nakute mo ii, -nakya / -nakucha with -nakereba naranai and -te wa ikenai shown as the SOURCES rather than as unmotivated later contractions, -nai to with ikenai routinely dropped so the sentence just trails off on '...to', -te mo concessive, INT + -te mo. Volitional: -oo / -yoo (nomoo, ikoo, tabeyoo, shiyoo, koyoo), -mashoo, -oo ka, -oo ka na. Request and prohibition paradigm: bare -te, -te kudasai (unpacked), -naide kudasai, -na (prohibitive, recognition), -e/-ro imperative (ike, shiro, mate, yamero, recognition only). tsumori da / yotei da.
stages.output: CONVERSATION ONSET at week 16 (month ~4): one 30-minute session per week, scaling to three by month 8. Gated on competence, not on hours — the 250-cumulative-listening-hours gate found in one source plan is arithmetically impossible at 1-2 h/day and gates on a channel that same plan calls decoration. Repair chunks must be automatic. Every failed retrieval in a live session is promoted to a production card the SAME DAY, regardless of the normal promotion rule: that is the highest-yield card in the system, because the retrieval need is already attested and the encoding is emotionally tagged.
stages.why: -tara is pulled far ahead of -eba, -to, and nara on pure frequency grounds and given six weeks alone, so that the collapse-to--tara outcome — which happens anyway when all four are taught adjacently — is achieved deliberately and correctly. Conversation opens at month 4 because earlier is a vocabulary lesson at the worst possible exchange rate, and later fossilizes a monologue-only competence: the irreplaceable thing conversation trains is backchannel timing, and reflexes cannot be built asynchronously.
stages.exitTest: 30 seconds of unscripted self-introduction and 5 unscripted personal answers with no English; >=70% content questions on unseen scripted dialogue at ~300 morae/min; obligation strength ladder ordered correctly (-tara doo < -ta hoo ga ii < -nakya < -nakereba naranai < beki).
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 12 min new, 30 min review, 18 min grammar drill, 5 min aizuchi, 20 min active listening, plus one 30-min live session/week.

stages.title: -te auxiliaries and the benefactive triangle
stages.trigger: Stage 12 exit.
stages.phonology: The mora-deleting reductions become production targets: chau (-2 morae from te shimau), toku (-1), teru (-1), teku (-1).
stages.grammar: -te shimau > -chau / -jau / -chatta / -jatta, with BOTH senses co-taught (regret and completion) — taught as 'regret' alone, tabechatta reads as apologetic; as 'completion' alone, wasurechatta loses its affect. The voicing follows the -te/-de split exactly. -te oku > -toku / -toita. -te miru. -te bakari iru. -te kuru / -te iku with ALL THREE senses co-present, because the spatial-only treatment leaves the far more frequent aspectual uses as noise: spatial (katte kuru, tsurete iku, motte iku), inceptive-toward-now (ame ga futte kita, wakatte kita, samuku natte kita, onaka ga suite kita), continuative-away-from-now (fuete iku, kawatte iku). motte kuru vs tsurete kuru — the thing/person split English collapses. THE BENEFACTIVE TRIANGLE as one indivisible unit: ageru / kureru / morau, then -te ageru / -te kureru / -te morau, then the register tiers yaru / kudasaru / itadaku / sashiageru. The request ladder laid out whole rather than one rung per level, because a learner who gets -te kudasai in month 2 and -te itadakemasen ka in month 14 never perceives them as points on a scale: -te / -te kudasai / -te kurenai? / -te moraeru? / -te kurenai kana / -te kuremasen ka / -te moraemasu ka / -te itadakemasen ka. -te hoshii / -te hoshikunai. The -te ageru trap: offering help with -te ageru sounds condescending; use -te mo ii desu ka or -mashoo ka. And the listening payoff: -te kureru grammatically forces a non-speaker subject, which makes it one of the principal cues for recovering dropped arguments at stage 18.
stages.output: Live conversation to 2 sessions/week. Retell drill immediately after the active-input block, harvesting the priming window (lexical and structural priming from comprehension to production is strong and lasts under an hour, so speech produced right after input reuses the constructions just heard and exposes gaps while the target is still audible).
stages.why: The benefactive system does structural work that English speakers expect from the passive, the possessive, and 'for me' — three things that are absent, rare, or wrong in Japanese. Delaying it, as Genki does across chapters 14 and 16, produces months of subtly cold, agentless output, and omitting kureru does not sound neutral, it sounds ungrateful. -chau and -toku are placed here, ahead of passive and causative, because in conversational audio -chau is clearly more frequent than the passive; the -toku frequency claim made in one source analysis is unsupported and is dropped — -toku earns its place on the decompression argument alone, since a listener who has not been told simply hears an unknown verb ending and stalls.
stages.exitTest: Request ladder produced at four politeness levels for 10 verbs; kureru vs ageru direction 20/20; -chau and -toku parsed in casual audio >=18/20; -te kuru three-sense assignment 15/15.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 12 min new, 32 min review, 15 min grammar drill, 5 min aizuchi, 20 min active listening, 10 min retell.

stages.title: Noun-modifying clauses: the ear-hard node
stages.trigger: Stages 9 and 12 both closed — the modifier must be buildable in all four tense/polarity cells plus the progressive. Passive exposure to modified nouns began at stage 10, six weeks before instruction.
stages.phonology: Downstep as a segmentation cue becomes the explicit tool: because pitch drops at most once per accentual phrase, every upward reset is positive evidence that a new phrase has begun — free word-boundary information in a stream with no spaces, and the actual return on the week-1 pitch investment.
stages.vocab: To ~2,700. The head-noun inventory finally admitted, having been deliberately withheld from week 3 where it would have been an untethered gloss: koto, mono, tokoro, toki, hito, yatsu (which casual speech uses constantly and no textbook teaches).
stages.grammar: [plain clause] + N in all four cells plus progressive: kinoo katta hon, mukoo de hanashiteru hito, ashita iku tokoro, tabetakunai mono. Clause-internal subject takes ga, or no in short clauses (watashi ga tsukutta ryoori / boku no katta hon). The head-final parsing drill with progressively longer modifiers — pure capacity work. The wa/ga diagnostic sharpened: bare wa CANNOT appear inside a relative, noun-complement, toki, or conditional clause, but it IS permitted before kara, kedo, and ga ('Tanaka-san wa konai kara, saki ni hajimeyoo'). The contrast between the two classes is better evidence for topic-vs-subject than the blanket ban usually taught, and the blanket ban is contradicted by input within days. toki (ni) with tense computed relative to the main clause: iku toki (before going) vs itta toki (after arriving). mae ni takes non-past always; ato de takes -ta always. aida / aida ni. -te iru aida ni.
stages.output: Live conversation 2/week. Active listening 25 min. The truncation drill runs at full strength: hear a clause with the final predicate complex clipped, predict polarity and tense; then full clauses of increasing length with polarity/tense questions only.
stages.why: Five days, the second-longest budget in the program, plus a background drilling track that continues to the end. English is head-initial and parsed incrementally with a relative pronoun and often a comma; Japanese is head-final with no relativizer, no comma, and in speech no prosodic break at all, so the listener must hold a complete-sounding predicate in working memory with no signal that it is subordinate. This responds to time-on-task, not to explanation. Textbooks budget one chapter and introduce it in READING, where visible word boundaries and the option to re-read hide how much harder the auditory version is.
stages.exitTest: >=8/10 content questions on 20 sentences carrying 3+ mora pre-nominal modifiers at 300 morae/min; iku toki vs itta toki tense questions 10/10; wa-permitted vs wa-banned subordinator classification >=18/20.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 12 min new, 32 min review, 20 min head-final parsing drill, 5 min aizuchi, 25 min active listening, 10 min retell.

stages.title: Nominalization, n da re-analyzed, quotation and the three -tte
stages.trigger: Stage 14 exit. Deliberately AFTER relative clauses, inverting the conventional order.
stages.phonology: The three homophonous no — genitive, nominalizer, explanatory — are an identical mora resolvable only from syntactic position, with no acoustic disambiguation whatsoever. A reader gets kanji and okurigana; a listener gets a drilled skill, and it belongs here rather than accumulating as confusion.
stages.grammar: no vs koto selection: perceptual, concrete, immediate > no; abstract, reported, idiomatic > koto, with the fixed frames koto ga aru, koto ga dekiru, koto ni suru, koto ni naru. THE COPULA ALLOMORPH TABLE, one rule that prevents a systematic error and is missing from every source analysis: na before no / n da / node / noni / hazu (gakusei na n da, kirei na no, byooki na node, gakusei na noni, gakusei na hazu); no before yoo da; BARE before mitai and rashii; da before soo da (hearsay). Without it the learner produces *gakusei da n da forever. n da / n desu / n ja nai? / n da kedo / n desu ka unpacked from the frozen status it held since week 3. Quotation: to omou, to iu, and the plain-form lock inside quotative complements regardless of the matrix clause's politeness. -TTE doing three jobs — to iu, quotative to, and topic wa — disambiguated only by position and prosody, and this is the audio-first payload, because spoken Japanese runs on -tte and textbooks introduce it, if at all, as slang. -tte iu / -tte itteta / -tte sa / -tte iwareta. Embedded questions: [clause] ka, ka doo ka. N to iu N and its contracted N tte N. -oo to omou / -oo to omotteru / -oo to suru / -oo to shita. -tagaru. Quotative hedges: -tte iu ka, tteka, mitai na, toka itte.
stages.output: Live conversation 3/week. Active listening 28 min, stepping to 330 morae/min.
stages.why: The reviewer correction that reorders two units. [clause]+no, [clause]+koto, ka doo ka, and N to iu N are ALL prenominal embedding — the same head-final, cue-free parse that stage 14 exists to train — so placing them first puts the dependent before its prerequisite. The edge runs one way only: nothing in nominalization or quotation is a prerequisite for relative clauses. And the plain-form lock inside quotative complements is the strongest single argument for the channel split at stage 6: a learner whose automatized form is -masu physically cannot build a quotative complement without unlearning their citation form.
stages.exitTest: >=18/20 disambiguating the three -tte by position; >=18/20 on the three no; copula allomorph correct in 10/10 elicited frames; produces n da appropriately in 10 elicited contexts.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 10 min new, 34 min review, 15 min grammar drill, 5 min aizuchi, 28 min active listening, 10 min retell.

stages.title: Clause linking, the remaining three conditionals, focus and comparison
stages.trigger: Stage 15 exit. -tara has now been the unmarked default for ten weeks.
stages.phonology: Sentence-final trailing contours: Japanese speakers routinely end a turn on kedo, kara, or -te with the second clause never uttered, which to an untrained ear sounds like a sentence that was cut off.
stages.grammar: kara (speaker-asserted reason) vs node (presented as given, softer); kedo / keredo / ga, plus kedo as a sentence-final softener; noni; shi; ja nakute; discourse connectives demo, dakara, sorede, soshite, jaa, tokorode, tteka. Key 5's other tail: -eba / -kereba (nomeba, tabereba, takakereba, nakereba), -eba ii, -eba yokatta (counterfactual regret, which is where -eba earns its keep), -eba -hodo. -TO with the constraint that actually generates errors, which every 'decision path' organized by register omits: -to cannot take a request, command, invitation, or volitional in the non-past main clause (*Massugu iku to, migi ni magatte kudasai). And the correction that matters — to-DISCOVERY IS available ('Uchi ni kaeru to, dare mo inakatta'), so 'discovery = tara only' is a false rule the learner will hear contradicted constantly. NARA: not an event conditional at all but uptake of a proposition already in play; it attaches to a bare noun (Biiru nara aru yo); and the sharpest drillable contrast in the system is temporal — iku nara (advice BEFORE going) vs ittara (AFTER arriving). -ba's own restriction, parallel to -to's and usually omitted: a verbal antecedent with a volitional or directive main clause is degraded. Focus and quantity: dake; shika...nai, taught as the SECOND member of a negative-polarity set whose first member (INT + mo: nanimo nai, daremo inai, dokonimo ikanai) the learner has owned since week 3, which makes it cheaper; bakari/bakkari; gurai/kurai; hodo; mo ('as many as'); sae; demo (ocha demo nomanai?); zutsu. Comparison, the deferred half of stage 10: A yori B no hoo ga, ichiban, A to B to docchi ga, onaji kurai, [N] hodo...nai, and the degree adverbs (totemo, sugoku, chotto, amari+NEG, zenzen+NEG, kanari, meccha, chou, hontoo ni).
stages.output: Live conversation 3/week. Active listening 32 min at 350 morae/min.
stages.why: None of the four conditionals depends on any other, so this is a free-choice node broken by frequency — and teaching them adjacently, as Genki II and every category-organized reference do, hands the learner a four-way selection problem before any single member is automatic. Two failure modes follow: freezing before every conditional, or collapsing to -tara with a residue of guilt. Giving -tara ten weeks alone achieves the collapse deliberately, and the selection procedure arrives when there is finally something to select between. The cost is that the -to discovery construction is unavailable for six months; accepted, because it is recognizable long before it is producible.
stages.exitTest: >=90% on a 40-item conditional-selection audio battery including 8 items testing the -to main-clause constraint and 5 testing iku nara vs ittara; shika...nai produced with obligatory negative in 5/5.
stages.dailyBraid: 10 min shadow, 10 min new, 35 min review, 15 min grammar drill, 5 min aizuchi, 32 min active listening, 10 min retell.

stages.title: Evidentials, modality, passive, and the transitivity pairs
stages.trigger: Stage 16 exit AND >=5 weeks elapsed since stage 11, the mandatory -eru separation. INPUT IGNITION also fires in this window on its own test.
stages.phonology: Fast-speech reduction now dominates the input; the mora-preserving substitutions become the focus (wakannai, sun no, samii).
stages.vocab: To ~4,200. Kango share rises from ~15% to ~40% of new items, carded in 2-4 mora collocation frames and batched homophone-aware — never two competing readings inside the same 200-item window (kikai opportunity vs kikai machine; kooen park vs kooen lecture; shiritsu private vs shiritsu municipal). The acoustic Sino-root heuristic is drilled before N+suru is licensed.
stages.grammar: EVIDENTIALS, the largest content gap in one source analysis and absent entirely: -soo (i-stem or adjective stem, APPEARANCE: oishisoo, furisoo, ochisoo, with the irregulars yosasoo and nasasoo) taught FIRST and alone; then mitai as the spoken workhorse (N mitai, [clause] mitai, mitai na N); then rashii (hearsay and typicality: ame rashii vs otoko rashii); then -ppoi; then soo da (plain clause + soo da, HEARSAY) introduced LATE as a direct minimal contrast against -soo appearance (ame ga furu soo da / ame ga furisoo da), because the two differ in what PRECEDES them and teaching them together by their shared syllable is how the confusion gets installed; yoo da demoted to recognition-only, inverting the textbook order that makes it the 'proper' form. Modality: deshoo / desho? / daroo with falling = conjecture and rising = seeking agreement; kamo (bare) rather than kamo shirenai; hazu / hazu ga nai / hazu datta noni; ni chigainai and wake da as recognition. The four 'should' as pair-then-append rather than a forced 2x2: -nakya (self-necessity) vs -ta hoo ga ii (advice) as the confusable pair first, then hazu appended (epistemic, belonging with daroo and kamo), then beki last as marked and moralizing. -garu / -tagaru with the constraint framed as FELICITY, not ungrammaticality: plain assertion about a third party's private state needs -garu/-soo/-rashii/-mitai/to omou, but questions to the ADDRESSEE are perfectly fine and far more frequent (Samui? Tabetai?) — teach the exemption first. PASSIVE: direct (sensei ni homerareta), adversative (ame ni furareta, tonari no hito ni sawagareta), possessor (saifu o nusumareta, ashi o fumareta, note the retained o), ni yotte for creation verbs, and the THIRD cell that ra-nuki does not remove and no source analysis lists — HONORIFIC -(ra)reru (shachoo ga kaeraremashita, moo yomaremashita ka), which is the most frequent -rareru in workplace and public speech. Three-way reconciliation keyed on animacy and target: inanimate subject or ni-agent > passive; ga-marked object > potential; social superior as subject with no agent > honorific. TRANSITIVITY PAIRS, ~30 core, batched by REAL alignment class rather than the false single alternation: -aru/-eru (shimaru/shimeru, kimaru/kimeru, atsumaru/atsumeru, tomaru/tomeru, sagaru/sageru, mitsukaru/mitsukeru, agaru/ageru), -u/-eru (aku/akeru, tsuku/tsukeru, todoku/todokeru — a large class the conventional taxonomy misfiles as irregular), -eru/-asu (kieru/kesu, deru/dasu, hieru/hiyasu), -ru/-su (naoru/naosu, nokoru/nokosu, mawaru/mawasu), -ku/-kasu (ugoku/ugokasu, kawaku/kawakasu), -reru/-su (kowareru/kowasu, taoreru/taosu), plus true irregulars hairu/ireru, ochiru/otosu, oriru/orosu, okiru/okosu, noru/noseru. The heuristic is WITHIN-pair only — the -aru member is intransitive, the -su/-asu member is transitive — and potential forms are explicitly excluded, because '-eru is transitive' mis-derives kieru, kowareru, deru, and every potential. The pairing is for discrimination, not generalization: which pattern a root takes is lexically listed, which is precisely why learners confuse them. -te aru (transitive result, unstated agent: mado ga akete aru) vs -te iru (intransitive result: mado ga aite iru). -te shimatta with intransitives.
stages.output: INPUT IGNITION TEST: 6 of 10 content questions on an unseen 90-second clip of natural dialogue at ~350 morae/min, two listens, no transcript, no rewind. On passing, active input goes from 32 min to uncapped and becomes the growth block. Live conversation 3/week.
stages.why: Transitivity pairs are gathered into one dedicated block rather than scattered because -te aru vs -te iru is unlearnable as a contrast unless you own a block of pairs simultaneously — the whole distinction turns on which member you picked. They are placed immediately after passive because Japanese uses intransitives where English uses the passive, so the contrast lands hardest when over-application of -rareru is fresh. And they are placed five weeks after potential because of the -eru collision, which is the single ordering constraint the source analyses most consistently violated.
stages.exitTest: Input ignition test passed. >=90% on a 40-pair transitive/intransitive selection battery with correct particle; adversative passive comprehension >=18/20; -soo appearance vs soo da hearsay >=18/20; three-way -rareru assignment >=16/20.
stages.dailyBraid: 8 min shadow, 10 min new, 36 min review, 15 min grammar drill, 5 min aizuchi, 35 min active input, 12 min retell.

stages.title: Causative, keigo capped, the spoken register layer, and the reduction system
stages.trigger: Stage 17 exit. Grammar terminates during this stage.
stages.phonology: The reduction system presented as a SYSTEM rather than a list, split by the two kinds. Mora-DELETING: te iru > teru, te oku > toku, te shimau > chau/jau, te wa > cha, de wa > ja, te iku > teku, nakereba > nakya, nakute wa > nakucha, to iu > tte, te ageru > tageru. Mora-PRESERVING segmental substitution, which needs a different drill because the rhythm is unchanged and only a segment shifts: ranai > nnai (wakannai, tsumannai), no > n (sonna no > sonna n, suru no > sun no), -ui > -ii (samii, atsii, warii), plus sugee, yabee, omoshiree. Fast-speech devoicing and deletion: des, shta, arimas, shitsurei shimas. Kansai recognition set of ~10 features, capped: akan, honma, -hen (wakarahen), ya / yanen, -toru (shitoru), nande yanen — with CHAU flagged for collision with the -chau auxiliary already installed (auxiliary chau is bound to a verb stem; Kansai chau stands alone or takes a nominal). Rendaku as a recognition multiplier, absent from every source analysis: hito > -bito, kami > -gami, hana > -bana, kuni > -guni, sake > -zake, fune > -bune, plus Lyman's Law, recovering hundreds of compounds from words already known.
stages.vocab: To ~5,000. Bound morpheme families as compression: -sha, -in (ten'in, ekiin, kaishain — note the moraic n before a vowel, a length contrast worth drilling), -shitsu, -kan, -ryoku (nooryoku, tairyoku, miryoku), -teki (kihonteki, gutaiteki, ippanteki), -ka, -chuu (vs -juu: kaigi-chuu vs ichinichi-juu, a length-and-voicing contrast on a suffix), -go/-zen (shokugo/shokuzen, gogo/gozen), -ppoi, -sa, fu-, mu-, sai-. -mi taught as a memorized list, not a rule.
stages.grammar: Causative -seru / -saseru with BOTH senses (coercion vs permission) and the constraint that is usually omitted: with a transitive verb the causee MUST be ni, because o is already taken (kodomo ni yasai o tabesaseta, never *kodomo o yasai o tabesaseta) — the o/ni contrast is free only for intransitives. The productive target is the frame, not the paradigm: -sasete kudasai / -sasete morau / -sasete itadaku, which is where nearly all real causative tokens live. -sasete oku. Causative-passive -saserareru > -sasareru, recognition only, with the restriction that the contraction is BLOCKED for -su stems (hanasaserareru, never *hanasasareru; likewise kesu, dasu). Why -te morau usually beats the causative for 'have someone do X'.
