KEIGO, capped at three days of production: ~15 sonkeigo and kenjoogo suppletives as recognition (irassharu, ossharu, nasaru, meshiagaru, goran ni naru, gozonji da, kudasaru; mairu, moosu, itadaku, haiken suru, ukagau, itasu, oru, zonjiru); gozaimasu / de gozaimasu, the single most-heard keigo frame in shops and stations; honorific -(ra)reru; o-/go- + i-stem + ni naru / suru as RECOGNITION ONLY, explicitly not drilled for production; ~8 production phrases (irasshaimase, shooshoo omachi kudasai, o-negai shimasu, kashikomarimashita, o-tsukaresama desu, shitsurei shimasu, itadakimasu, yoroshiku onegaishimasu). o-/go- STRIPPING as a parsing multiplier: recognition-only cards, audio prompt, answer is the bare stem, preventing several hundred words from registering as false unknowns. THE SPOKEN REGISTER LAYER, which contains almost nothing found in a standard beginner curriculum and is the most important unit in the second half: the full final-particle set (ne, yo, yo ne, na, naa, sa, zo, ze, wa, kke, mon, jan, desho, no-rising); fillers (eeto, anoo, maa, nanka, yappari, sono, nan te iu ka); aizuchi at natural density with juncture triggers; PARTICLE ELLIPSIS and role recovery from word order, animacy, and verb semantics; ZERO ANAPHORA and its four recovery cues — benefactive direction (-te kureru forces a non-speaker subject), honorific level, -tai (first person only), -tagaru (non-first person); postposing ('sugoi yo, sore'); trailing on -te/-kedo/-kara.
stages.output: Grammar block goes 15 min > 0. Active input takes the whole 15 minutes. Live conversation 3/week. Plain-form PRODUCTION begins here, roughly eight months after plain-form comprehension, once the learner has modeled enough real interaction to know who it is safe with.
stages.why: Keigo has almost no fanout — nothing in the graph depends on it — and its productive use by a non-native adult outside a customer-facing job is rare, while its recognition burden is unavoidable. So the split is sharp and the receptive half was already delivered at week 5. Curricula that drill productive keigo at the end of the beginner sequence spend weeks on a skill exercised approximately never, while particle ellipsis and zero anaphora, which every single conversation exercises, get nothing. The register layer is the direct answer: a learner trained only on fully-specified textbook sentences can parse textbook sentences and nothing else.
stages.exitTest: GRAMMAR TERMINATES: >=90% on a 140-item unseen audio battery at natural speed with no rewind, covering conditionals x4, potential, passive x3 uses, causative, causative-passive, te-auxiliaries, benefactives, nominalizers, evidentials, adjective inflection, volitional, request/prohibition, obligation, comparison, and counters. HARD CEILING month 9 whether or not passed; re-test monthly thereafter. Also: parses 20 particle-stripped, argument-dropped utterances at >=16/20.
stages.dailyBraid: 8 min shadow, 10 min new, 36 min review, 12 min grammar (to 0), 5 min aizuchi, 40 min active input, 12 min retell.

stages.title: Input dominance, frequency-list exhaustion, and the switch to mining
stages.trigger: Grammar retired. Unknown-word rate in real target material below ~15 per 10 minutes. Median card latency, measured from clip OFFSET, under 1.2 s.
stages.phonology: Quarterly perceptual re-audit with entirely new talkers and new carrier frames, because re-testing on trained voices measures memory rather than category, and discrimination gains decay silently under vocabulary load — subjective confidence does not track accuracy. The kite/kiite/kitte three-way is re-run as a hard gate each time.
stages.vocab: ~6,000 recognized crossed around month 12-13 — NOT month 9, because the corrected review-load arithmetic caps N at 20/day, and because roughly a quarter of the 6,000 arrives free from multipliers (N+suru over ~800-1000 Sino-Japanese nouns, the i-stem tails, o-/go- stripping, rendaku, the ka/mo/demo paradigm, the morpheme families, the kosoado grid) rather than from cards. New cards then TAPER AS A CLIFF, not a glide: 20 > 5 > 0 over three weeks, because the short-interval steps carry almost all the review cost and a glide keeps refilling them. Load drops 40-60% within 3-5 weeks and then trails. Source switches from frequency list to mining at 5-10/day: collocations (ki ni naru, ki ni suru, ki o tsukeru, shikata ga nai, tori aezu, yappari, ichioo, sono uchi, nan to naku, tonikaku), mimetics (which are cheap by ear because reduplication and sound symbolism make them memorable, and opaque on the page — the exact inverse of kango, which is why a reading-ordered curriculum defers them and an ear-ordered one promotes them: chanto, yukkuri, bikkuri, hakkiri, dandan, zutto, pekopeko, perapera, dokidoki, wakuwaku, iraira, gakkari, shikkari, barabara, girigiri, bochibochi), register-marked variants from the learner's own domains, and failure-triggered items from conversation logs.
stages.grammar: Lookup only. Monthly re-test on the residual battery items; the usual residue is -saserareru, wake da vs hazu da, adversative passive, and -tara vs -to in counterfactuals. The opaque compound tails arrive here as ~60 memorized LEXICAL items, not a rule: -dasu (hashiridasu, omoidasu), -komu (kangaekomu, mooshikomu, norikomu), -kiru (tsukaikiru), -naosu (yarinaosu), -au (hanashiau, shiriau), -kakeru (iikakeru), -nuku, -sokonau. Presenting them as a rule causes over-generation into forms nobody says, and there is no negative evidence in the input to correct it.
stages.output: Active input 45 min/day and rising, at 380-420 morae/min. Live conversation 3-4/week. Mining pipeline: flag in input > card by evening > production promotion if it recurs or if it was reached for and missed live.
stages.why: Two things happen at once and they are causally linked. Past rank ~6,000 the next thousand list items have a lower expected encounter rate than the words the learner is actually meeting, so encounter-driven mining strictly dominates. And stopping new cards makes the review load self-liquidate, handing back roughly 25 minutes/day at precisely the moment input becomes the bottleneck. That decay was engineered by capping and then cliffing rather than spreading evenly — a flat schedule holds the load constant forever and never produces a phase where input dominates.
stages.exitTest: >=85% content-question accuracy on unseen 380 morae/min natural conversation; unknown-word rate below 8 per 10 minutes in the learner's chosen domains; review block under 20 min/day.
stages.dailyBraid: 5 min shadow warmup, 8 min mining cards, 22 min review, 45 min active input, 20 min output (retell + conversation prep). Passive input off-clock.

stages.title: The latency phase: output dominance and speed
stages.trigger: Comprehension no longer the binding constraint (>=85% at 380 morae/min), and production latency measurably lagging comprehension. The metric switches here.
stages.phonology: Accent production finally held to a standard, having been allowed to lag perception by more than a year. Compound deaccenting (Tookyoo daigaku, nihongo) and modifier-plus-noun forming one accentual phrase with a single drop.
stages.vocab: Mining only, 5-8/day, drawn from encounter rather than list. Steady-state review block ~15 min.
stages.grammar: Nothing explicit. The residual battery is re-tested quarterly and the gaps close incidentally.
stages.output: THE METRIC IS NO LONGER CARDS KNOWN. Cards carry a response deadline measured from clip offset (fail at >1.2 s for 2-4 mora items). Input speed steps 380 > 420 > 450+ morae/min into unscripted MULTI-PARTY speech, because that is where overlap, particle drop, and reduction actually live and where a news-reading pace never takes you. The primary gating task is continuous shadowing at 380+ morae/min with a lag under 1 second — a better instrument than card latency, which is unmeasurable as usually specified. The retell drill sits immediately after the input block, exploiting the priming window, and is the highest-yield single exercise in the phase. Live conversation 3-4/week plus self-recording, transcription by ear, and gap analysis against the model. HARD RULE, enforced monthly: if listening comprehension does not improve for six consecutive weeks while vocabulary grows by 1,000+, halve new cards that week — a large deck with a sub-800 ms card latency and sub-50% real-speech comprehension is a speed deficit, and adding cards cannot touch it.
stages.why: SRS trains recognition with unlimited time and rewards you for using it; comprehension of running speech requires recognition under a hard deadline, because access must complete in a few hundred milliseconds or the parse falls behind and collapses. These are different skills over the same knowledge. The characteristic failure mode of this phase is a comfortable plateau — comprehension becomes good enough to enjoy content, so effort stops — and the countermeasure is a metric that keeps producing a moving number after comprehension has stopped producing one.
stages.exitTest: Continuous shadowing at 420 morae/min with lag under 1 s for 3 minutes; >=80% content questions on unscripted three-party conversation at 450 morae/min; holds a 20-minute unscripted conversation with correct aizuchi density and no English repair; produces plain and polite registers appropriately without a switching pause.
stages.dailyBraid: 5 min shadow warmup, 8 min mining, 15 min review, 45 min active input at stepped speed, 27 min output (retell, self-recording, conversation). Live sessions 3-4/week.

contestedCalls.question: Does the -te form land at day 22 (the pure dependency-graph answer) or at week 9 (after a phonology block and an induction base)?
contestedCalls.verdict: Week 9, day ~60. Later than the fanout argument alone would put it, and roughly six weeks earlier than any textbook.
contestedCalls.why: The fanout argument is correct — the -te form has ~35 direct dependents and unlocking it converts a large share of spoken verb tokens from noise into structure — but the day-22 answer assumes two things that are false for this learner. First, there is no validated ear at day 22, and the -te alternations are precisely a gemination-and-voicing chant, so drilling them on uncalibrated categories installs the wrong motor program at volume. Second, and decisively, the conventional induction set (taberu, iku, suru, kuru) contains one ichidan verb, both irregulars, and the single verb that violates the -ku > -ite rule. It cannot teach the five-way chant at all. Waiting for >=4 regular godan verbs per coda class costs four weeks and is what makes the chant a rule rather than a table.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: Four extra weeks in which a third of verb tokens stay unparseable — real, and the missed listening exposure is not recoverable. Mitigated because the pre-teaching stores those verbs as (dictionary, -te) audio pairs from week 5, so the learner can already parse tabete and itta before the rule exists; the chant at week 9 is compressing data they already hold, which is why it takes 10 days instead of 4 weeks.

contestedCalls.question: Is the vocabulary target 6,000 words by month 9 at 30 new cards/day, as the front-loading argument concludes?
contestedCalls.verdict: No. N caps at 20/day and 6,000 recognized items lands at month 12-13. The 30/day figure rests on arithmetic that is wrong by roughly 3x.
contestedCalls.why: The standard model computes steady-state reviews as new-per-day times the sum of reciprocal intervals, which gives ~2.2N. But a card occupies interval step I_k for I_k days and generates exactly one review to leave it, so each step contributes N reviews/day once filled — reviews scale with the COUNT of ladder steps reached, not the sum of their reciprocals. Ladder {1 day, 100 days}, N=1: the reciprocal model predicts ~1 review/day, reality after 1,000 days is ~10. Corrected, steady state is ~6-7N, and at ~5 s comprehension presses, ~15 s production presses on 40% of items, plus encoding, one new card per day costs roughly 2 minutes per day forever. At N=30 that is over an hour of a 90-minute budget before any input, output, or shadowing. Audio-first makes it worse, not better, because Sino-Japanese homophony forces collocation-length cards for a large share of the lexicon.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: If the true cost is lower, the learner has budget headroom and can raise N — a pleasant discovery, cheaply corrected. If the plan had kept 30/day, the outcome is the single highest-attrition event in self-directed study: around month 9 the daily review count arrives at three to four times what was budgeted, the session runs two and a half hours, two days are missed, and a 900-card backlog ends the project. The multipliers are how the 6,000 target survives the cap: roughly a quarter of it arrives free from rules rather than from cards.

contestedCalls.question: Potential and the transitivity pairs both want the -eru slot. Which goes first, and how far apart?
contestedCalls.verdict: Potential at week 13, transitivity pairs at month 8. Minimum five weeks apart, both carded in full frames with the particle.
contestedCalls.why: This is the sharpest conflict between the source dimensions and both got it wrong in opposite directions. The dependency graph chains potential to -eba at week 14 because they share the e-stem — pure morphological tidiness, which is exactly the pedagogical-symmetry tiebreak that fanout-weighting rejects everywhere else, and it delays a top-tier conversational function by six weeks. The interference analysis moves potential earlier but schedules transitivity one week before it, producing the tightest homophone collision in that plan. The collision is real and systematic: the -eru potential of a godan verb is homophonous with the -eru transitive member of a pair — kaeru (can buy) vs kaeru (change), kireru (is cut) vs kireru (can cut), and the same for yakeru, toreru, wareru, nukeru. Inflection does not separate them, because the potential is itself an ichidan verb with an identical -te form. The only surviving cue in the audio stream is argument structure: potential takes ga, transitive takes o.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: If five weeks is insufficient, the learner carries a ga/o hesitation on a few dozen verbs, correctable with framed re-drilling. If the two were adjacent, the result is a permanently ambiguous -eru class that the ear cannot resolve and that no amount of later spacing repairs, because the interference happened at encoding.

contestedCalls.question: Do relative clauses come before or after nominalization and quotation?
contestedCalls.verdict: Before. Relative clauses at weeks 18-20, nominalization and quotation at months 5.5-6.5.
contestedCalls.why: [clause] + no, [clause] + koto, ka doo ka, and N to iu N are all prenominal embedding — the identical head-final, cue-free parse that the relative-clause unit exists to train. Scheduling them first puts the dependent before its prerequisite by the plan's own mechanism, and the edge runs one way only: nothing in nominalization or quotation is a prerequisite for relative clauses. The reason every curriculum inverts this is that nominalization looks like a small vocabulary item on the page while relative clauses look like syntax; by ear the difficulty ranks the other way.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: n da and to omou — both very high frequency — would arrive later than their frequency deserves. Mitigated directly: n da is admitted at week 3 as a frozen four-cell sentence-final pattern (n da / n desu / n ja nai? / n da kedo) with a scheduled unpack at stage 15, since its internal structure is invisible to a listener anyway. That is chunk-before-parse applied to a grammar point, and it costs one card.

contestedCalls.question: Is ra-nuki the citation form for the potential, as two source analyses claim?
contestedCalls.verdict: Calibrated by stem length, not adopted wholesale. Ra-nuki (tabereru, mireru, koreru, dereru) for 1-2 mora ichidan stems and kuru; -rareru for 3+ mora stems (oshierareru, kangaerareru, oboerareru).
contestedCalls.why: The blanket claim that ra-nuki 'dominates across most age groups' is overstated. Survey data puts it at roughly parity for short high-frequency ichidan verbs with a strong age gradient, and well under parity for longer stems, where it is markedly rare and stigmatized. Teaching *oshiereru as the citation form produces a form the learner will essentially never hear. The genuine argument for ra-nuki survives untouched and is not frequency but disambiguation: -rareru is syncretic across potential, passive, and honorific, and assigning tabereru to potential removes the ambiguity from the productive system where it is dense. But it does not remove it entirely — honorific -(ra)reru remains, and it is the most frequent -rareru in workplace and public speech, which is why the three-way reconciliation at stage 17 is keyed on animacy and honorific target rather than the two-way one both source analyses proposed.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: A mild register marking in formal settings on a handful of short verbs, invisible in casual speech and forgiven in a non-native speaker. The alternative failure — a -rareru that is ambiguous three ways for an ear-only learner with no orthographic fallback — is a comprehension bug that takes years to clear.

contestedCalls.question: Does pitch accent gate the start of vocabulary, ride on the cards, or get deferred to immersion?
contestedCalls.verdict: It does not gate, but it is a card-format constraint from card 1, and it is trained in two separate tracks: per-word accent tags on every item, and a phrase-level downstep track on running speech from week 3.
contestedCalls.why: Length is phonemic and functionally loaded, so a fuzzy length category destroys lexical identity and must gate. Accent is a per-word lexical property, acquired far more cheaply distributed across 6,000 items than concentrated in a 60-pair battery, and gating on it adds three to five weeks for a contrast that does not transfer from isolated pairs to connected speech. But two corrections make it non-optional at card 1. First, heiban and odaka are acoustically IDENTICAL on the bare word, so every noun must be recorded as 'X ga' from item 1 or the entire deck needs re-recording later. Second — and this is the synthesis move that pays for itself — accent RELEASES a large set of items that the interference analysis wanted to defer by months. kaeru [1] vs kaeru [0], kiru [1] vs kiru [0], atsui [2] vs atsui [0], omoi [0] vs omoi [2] are accent minimal pairs, not unlearnable homophones, so they are trained in the phonology block instead of separated. Only the genuinely accent-identical collisions get the separation treatment. And pitch PERCEPTION is a segmentation skill, not a naturalness polish: because pitch drops at most once per accentual phrase, every upward reset marks a phrase boundary, which is free word-boundary information in a stream with no spaces.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: If the accent tags turn out unreliable — a real risk, since off-the-shelf Japanese TTS is unreliable on lexical accent, which is why pipeline validation is stage 0 — the learner has spent a few minutes per week on a field that is noise. If accent were deferred instead, every noun acquired before it needs re-encoding plus re-recording, and adult accent errors once consolidated are among the most persistent L2 errors there are.

contestedCalls.question: Should there be a hard vocabulary threshold before any grammar, and what is it?
contestedCalls.verdict: Yes, but stated as an induction base rather than a word count: >=500 recognized words, >=150 chunks, and >=40 verbs already stored as (dictionary, -te) audio pairs with >=4 per godan coda class. That lands at week 6-7, not the conventional 800-word / month-2.5 gate.
contestedCalls.why: The argument for a gate is right and the metric is wrong. A grammar drill is slot-filling; if the fillers are unknown, every repetition does double duty as a vocabulary lesson, attention goes to the novel lexical item, and the pattern gets indexed to the words it was drilled with rather than abstracted — roughly halving throughput. But 800 is arbitrary. What actually matters is whether the induction set can support the generalization, and for the -te chant it demonstrably cannot at any word count if the set is taberu, iku, suru, kuru. Gating on the base rather than the count also buys back a week and a half, which goes straight to the -te subtree.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: If the gate is too loose, the -te chant is drilled shallowly and needs a second pass — one week. If grammar had started day 1 alongside the first hundred words, as every classroom curriculum does, the four-month closed-set sprint stretches to seven or eight, which is the difference between retiring grammar at month 9 and never retiring it.

contestedCalls.question: Which corpus ranks the vocabulary, and does it matter?
contestedCalls.verdict: CEJC (Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation) primary, with the Nagoya University Conversation Corpus and drama subtitle counts secondary. NOT the CSJ, and not any written corpus.
contestedCalls.why: This corrects a fatal instrument error. One source analysis names the CSJ as the ranking authority while recommending a list the CSJ would not produce. The CSJ is roughly three-quarters academic presentation and simulated public speech — spontaneous in the sense of unscripted, not in the sense of conversational. Lecture monologue is exactly the register that is dense in shikashi, mata, sarani, tsumari, and abstract kango, and thin in yo ne, kke, -chau, meccha, tteka. Ranking against it would produce close to the inverse of the intended list. The general principle survives and is the load-bearing one: rank against genuine dialogue, and treat a high written rank with a low spoken rank as evidence AGAINST early inclusion, not as neutral.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: If the dialogue corpora are less available or smaller than the CSJ, the fallback is subtitle counts from contemporary drama, which are noisier but register-correct. Ranking against a lecture corpus while believing it is conversation is the worse error, because it is invisible: the list looks empirically grounded and is systematically wrong at exactly the top of the distribution, where function words and interactional particles live.

contestedCalls.question: Do numbers and counters go early, late, or as one topic at all?
contestedCalls.verdict: Split them and put both earlier than the source analyses did. Numbers, the -tsu series, dates, and times as a week 5-8 sprint; counters restricted to ten counters at cells 1-6 plus the nan- interrogative — about 56 items, not 300.
contestedCalls.why: Three of the five source analyses omit this entirely, which is the largest shared gap in all of them. Counters are a closed set saturated with sound changes that exist ONLY in speech — ippon/sanbon/roppon/happon, ikkai/sangai/rokkai/jukkai, ippun/sanpun/roppun/juppun, tsuitachi/futsuka/yokka/hatsuka, yoji/kuji/shichiji — and they are unavoidable in the first real conversations an adult beginner can have. They are also cheap for this learner specifically: the alternations are obstruent-triggered gemination and nasal-triggered voicing, the same phonology as the -te chant, and they drill as a rhythm in twenty minutes. The split is by cost of error: mishearing a number in a transaction costs money, using the wrong counter costs a mild oddity. So numbers get full memorization and the counter tail gets none, with the -tsu series as the escape hatch. The one adjustment to the source recommendations: rehearse cells 1-6, not 1-3, because four and five are ordinary in ordering and shopping.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: If counters are needed earlier than month 2, they are individually cheap to add on demand precisely because they are being learned as cells rather than as a system. The rejected early-and-complete approach costs weeks of SRS time on kyuuhon and nanahiki, forms that will not be uttered in a decade.

contestedCalls.question: How much passive and causative is taught productively, and when?
contestedCalls.verdict: Both at month 8, both narrow. Passive productive only in the adversative and possessor frames; causative productive only inside -sasete kudasai / -sasete morau / -sasete itadaku. Causative-passive recognition only.
contestedCalls.why: Every mainstream curriculum treats these as the summit of the beginner course and spends four to six weeks drilling them productively. In conversational audio the passive plausibly loses a frequency contest to -chau, which those curricula never teach at all — and the functions English speakers reach for the passive to express are handled in Japanese by benefactives and intransitive verbs, both of which this sequence teaches earlier and drills harder. In real speech the overwhelming majority of causative tokens sit inside permission-seeking frames, not coercion, so that is the productive target. Two constraints usually omitted are included: with a transitive verb the causee must be ni, because o is already taken; and the -sasareru contraction is blocked for -su stems.
contestedCalls.ifWrong: A learner who ends up in a Japanese workplace finds their passive stiff and their causative confined to one frame — recoverable in a few weeks of targeted work once the need is real. The alternative spends five weeks of the sprint on constructions that lose to -chau, and crowds out the register and reduction work that every single conversation exercises.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Teaches -masu for the first 8-14 chapters (Genki reveals plain form at ch. 8, Minna no Nihongo at L20), presenting plain form later as 'casual speech'. Runs the same sequence for comprehension and production.
againstStandard.weDo: Split by channel. Plain form is the comprehension citation form from the first verb at week 6; production runs on a -masu/-desu shell for the first four months on social-risk grounds, and plain-form production begins at month 9. The shell is the i-stem plus five endings, and naming the i-stem there is what makes twenty later constructions free.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Every subordinate clause has to be relearned, so the plain-form chapter feels like restarting the course, and learners produce *tabemasu toki, *ikimasu to omoimasu, *kaimashita hon for months. It also doubles the card count by teaching the same nodes in two shells, which is the overhead that makes a four-month grammar sprint impossible. Note the usual justification for this correction is overstated and we do not repeat it: plain form is obligatory in prenominal, quotative, nominalized, and conditional/temporal positions — about 25 constructions — but -masu is fully grammatical before kara, node, kedo, ga, and shi.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Places the -te form at Genki ch. 6 or Minna no Nihongo L14 — roughly month 3 at classroom pace — and teaches it as a five-row table keyed to kana columns, with an induction set of taberu, iku, suru, kuru.
againstStandard.weDo: Week 9, ten days, drilled as a chant to production speed under 300 ms, on an induction base of at least four regular godan verbs per coda class, with iku deliberately excluded from the set and taught afterward as the sole exception. -ta comes free as the same slot with the final vowel swapped e to a.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Eight or more weeks in which roughly a third of spoken verb tokens are unparseable, and the compounding loss is listening exposure, which cannot be recovered later. Separately, the conventional induction set contains one ichidan verb, both irregulars, and the one verb that violates the -ku rule — not a single regular godan verb — so it cannot teach the generalization at all and produces a memorized table that fails under time pressure, which is exactly where it matters.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Treats contractions (-teru, -chau, -toku, -nakya, -cha, -ja, -tte) as slang, a 'casual speech' chapter, or an appendix. Most Anki decks put the long form on the answer side.
againstStandard.weDo: The contracted form IS the citation form at the point of introduction, with the long form taught alongside as the formal expansion. Then a dedicated systematizing pass at month 10 that splits the mora-DELETING reductions (te iru > teru, te shimau > chau, te oku > toku, te iku > teku) from the mora-PRESERVING segmental substitutions (wakaranai > wakannai, suru no > sun no, -ui > -ii), because only the first is a shortening and the second needs a different drill.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Catastrophic specifically for an audio-first learner: the trained representations never match the signal, so every act of listening carries a decompression tax paid under real-time pressure, and decompression is the first thing that fails under load. The learner hears tabechatta and cannot recover taberu, hears -tte and cannot recover to iu.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Skips phonology entirely, or reduces it to 'Japanese has only five vowels, it's easy for English speakers'. Where phonology is covered, it is inside a kana lesson, so an audio-first learner who skips kana receives none of it. Devoicing is taught on day 1 as 'desu is really des'.
againstStandard.weDo: A 10-14 day pre-vocabulary block with a hard four-week ceiling and a tiered exit. Isochrony on all-CV words first, because length is a ratio and needs a stable denominator. Fricative geminates before stop geminates, because one cue is audible friction and the other is a beat of silence. Devoicing LAST, at day 11-13, framed as perception with the beat explicitly preserved. Accent tagged on every card and every noun recorded with -ga.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Every word encoded before the categories exist is stored with a corrupted phonological representation that the SRS then rehearses hundreds of times — reviews reinforce the blur, they do not repair it. The day-1 devoicing tip is worse than useless: an English speaker deletes the mora along with the voicing, because English has no way to represent a beat with no voiced nucleus, and since -masu is on every polite verb this mis-times a large fraction of everything they will ever say.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Clusters the four conditionals (-tara, -ba, -to, nara) into one or two adjacent chapters, and states the selection rule in terms of register or translation.
againstStandard.weDo: -tara alone at week 15, free from the -ta chant, with ten weeks to become the unmarked default. -eba, -to, and nara at month 7 with the constraints that actually generate errors: -to bans a request, command, invitation, or volitional in the non-past main clause; -ba is degraded with a volitional main clause and same subjects; nara does not assert its antecedent and attaches to bare nouns; iku nara means before going while ittara means after arriving. And the correction that matters — to-discovery IS available in the past tense, so 'discovery equals tara only' is a false rule the learner will hear contradicted within days.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: A four-way selection problem handed to the learner before any single member is automatic, producing either a freeze before every conditional or a silent collapse onto -tara with a residue of guilt. The forms are also learned apart from their real jobs, so -eba never attaches to counterfactual regret and nara never attaches to discourse uptake.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Treats passive and causative as the summit of the beginner course (Genki II ch. 21-23, Minna L37/L48) with four to six weeks of productive drilling, causative-passive as the capstone. Never teaches -chau or -toku.
againstStandard.weDo: Both at month 8 and both narrow: passive productive only in the adversative and possessor frames, causative productive only inside -sasete kudasai / -sasete morau / -sasete itadaku, causative-passive recognition only with the -su-stem blocking noted. -chau and -toku are taught four months earlier, at week 16.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Five or six weeks of a nine-month sprint spent on constructions that plausibly lose a conversational frequency contest to -chau, which those curricula never teach at all. It also crowds out the register and reduction work that every single conversation exercises. And the standard treatment omits the constraint that with a transitive verb the causee must be ni, so learners produce the ungrammatical double-o causative.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Organizes vocabulary into thematic sets — colors, days of the week, family terms, body parts, classroom objects — and scatters transitive/intransitive verb pairs across sixty chapters as ordinary vocabulary as they happen to come up.
againstStandard.weDo: Randomized conversational-frequency order with thematic grouping banned, EXCEPT for five rule-bearing contrast families that are deliberately blocked into one session: transitivity pairs, the four conditionals, ageru/kureru/morau, the -te auxiliary family, and phonological minimal pairs. Transitivity pairs get one dedicated block of ~30 at month 8, batched by the real alignment classes.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Semantic clusters compete on near-identical retrieval cues, costing roughly 25-30% more repetitions plus persistent within-set confusions (hidari/migi, kayoobi/kin'yoobi, ani/ane) that survive into speech. Meanwhile scattering the transitivity pairs makes -te aru vs -te iru unlearnable, because the entire distinction turns on which member you picked and the contrast is invisible until you own a block simultaneously — which is also the main reason English speakers over-apply the passive. Note the usual justification for pairing them is wrong and we do not repeat it: there is no single productive -aru/-eru alternation, the system has 15+ patterns, and which one a root takes is lexically listed. Pair them for discrimination, not generalization.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Omits sentence-final particles beyond a paragraph on ne and yo, omits aizuchi, fillers, particle ellipsis, and zero anaphora, or demotes them to a culture note. Never mentions particle-dropping because textbook sentences never drop particles. Where backchanneling is taught, it is taught as a clock interval.
againstStandard.weDo: Final particles drip from week 3 and get a full inventory at month 9; particle ellipsis is drilled explicitly from week 4 with the elliptical version as the production target; zero anaphora gets its four recovery cues taught as a skill (benefactive direction, honorific level, -tai first-person, -tagaru non-first-person); and aizuchi is drilled against JUNCTURES — clause-final particles, pauses, terminal contours — graded on landing within ~300 ms, from month 3.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Two separate injuries. Production is grammatical and robotic, and failing to backchannel at Japanese rates causes interlocutors to stop and check whether you are still there. Comprehension is far worse: real speech drops the topic, the object, and the particles, so a learner trained only on fully-specified sentences can parse textbooks and nothing else. And the clock-timed backchannel drill actively teaches the learner to interrupt mid-clause, which is worse than silence.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Orders vocabulary by a written-language frequency list — JLPT levels, newspaper corpora, BCCWJ, or any kanji-graded 'core 2k/6k' deck — and front-loads Sino-Japanese because it looks efficient and makes the word count climb fast. Splits homophones by kanji.
againstStandard.weDo: Rank against genuine dialogue corpora. Roughly 85:15 wago to kango through the first 1,000 items, flipping to about 40:60 by 6,000, with early kango screened for low homophone competition and batched so no two competing readings fall inside the same 200-item window. Wago cards are bare audio; kango cards carry a 2-4 mora collocation frame. Merge orthographic splits that are phonologically and accentually identical, split ones that are not.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: The learner arrives at 2,000 words knowing shikashi, sarani, keizai, and de aru, and not knowing yappari, nanka, -chau, yo ne, kke, or bochibochi — and because the missing items are function words and discourse particles rather than content words, the gap does not close with more listening, it blocks listening. Front-loading kango is worse for an ear-only learner specifically: it is 2-morae-by-2 with heavy long vowels and geminates, so homophone density is extreme and the kanji that disambiguates on the page does nothing at all in the ear. Kanji-driven sense splits (three atsui) produce cards with literally identical prompts, which are unlearnable by construction and become permanent leeches.

againstStandard.standardDoes: Never terminates grammar study, rolling from N5 to N4 to N3 to N2 pattern books indefinitely; and drills productive keigo (o-V-ni naru, o-V-suru, the full suppletive system) as the capstone of the beginner sequence.
againstStandard.weDo: Grammar terminates on a 140-item unseen audio battery at natural speed, expected month 8-9, with a hard ceiling at month 9 whether or not it is passed and monthly re-tests thereafter. Keigo is split by channel: the receptive service-encounter script is installed at week 5, roughly a year earlier than any standard plan; the ~15 suppletives, gozaimasu, and honorific -(ra)reru are recognition only; the productive o-V-ni naru template is explicitly never drilled; eight frozen phrases get production cards.
againstStandard.costOfStandard: Roughly 200 hours across two years on patterns whose real-world encounter rate is below one per ten hours of speech — time that would have bought 200 hours of listening. And several weeks on a productive skill a non-native adult outside a customer-facing job will exercise approximately never, while the keigo they cannot avoid hearing in every shop, station, and train announcement is not installed until month 20. Also note the standard closed-set list is not closed: it routinely omits adjective inflection, the volitional, the request and prohibition paradigm, obligation forms, comparison, question words including nande, and the entire numeral-and-counter system.
